actionRequired.description:
Action required for the custom scheduler plugin developers. 
Here's the breaking change in `EnqueueExtension` in the scheduling framework. 
The `EventsToRegister` in `EnqueueExtension` changed the return value from `ClusterEvent` to `ClusterEventWithHint`. `ClusterEventWithHint` allows each plugin to filter out more useless events via the callback function named `QueueingHintFn`.
When the scheduling queue receives a cluster event, before moving each Pod from unschedulable pod pool to activeQ/backoffQ, it will call QueueingHintFn of plugins that rejected each Pod in the previous scheduling cycle.
Depending on the value returned from QueueingHintFn, the scheduling queue changes how it queues each Pod:
- if more than one QueueingHintFn returns QueueImmediately, it queues Pod to activeQ.
- If no QueueingHintFn returns QueueImmediately and more than one plugin returns QueueAfterBackoff, it queues Pod to backoffQ if Pod is backing off, or to activeQ if Pod's backoff has already finished.
- If all QueueingHintFn return QueueSkip, it puts this pod back to the unschedulable pod pool

Having appropriate QueueingHintFn contributes to reducing useless retries and thus improves the overall scheduler's performance.

**How can I migrate?**

For backward compatibility, nil `QueueingHintFn` is treated as always returning QueueAfterBackoff. 
So, if you want to just keep the existing behavior, you can register `ClusterEventWithHint` with no `QueueingHintFn` in it. 
But, registering appropriate `QueueingHintFn` is, of course, better from a scheduling performance perspective.
actionRequired.author: sanposhiho

enrichment.title: EnqueueExtension return type changed
enrichment.summary: The `EnqueueExtension` method now returns `ClusterEventWithHint` instead of `ClusterEvent`; plugins must update to register this type and optionally implement `QueueingHintFn` for better queue handling.
enrichment.action: Modify custom scheduler plugins to use the new `ClusterEventWithHint` return type in `EnqueueExtension`. For backward compatibility you may pass a nil `QueueingHintFn` (behaves as `QueueAfterBackoff`), but implementing an appropriate `QueueingHintFn` is recommended to improve scheduling performance.

bugOrRegression.author: brianpursley

issueContext.title: $deleteFromPrimitiveList keeps elements instead of removing them
issueContext.body:
### What happened?

This page explains that the deleteFromPrimitiveList should delete the specified items, but the specified items are kept, and the other items are deleted.

https://github.com/kubernetes/community/blob/master/contributors/devel/sig-api-machinery/strategic-merge-patch.md#deletefromprimitivelist-directive



### What did you expect to happen?

The specified items in the deleteFromPrimitiveList should be removed.


### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

```
$ cat <<EOF > deploy1.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nginx
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nginx
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nginx
    spec:
      containers:
      - image: nginx
        name: nginx
        args:
        - "--debug"
        - "--other-param"
EOF

$ kubectl apply -f deploy1.yaml

$ kubectl  patch deployments nginx --type=strategic \
-p '{ "spec":{ "template":{ "spec":{ "containers":[ { "name":"nginx", "$deleteFromPrimitiveList/args": [ "--debug" ]}]}}}}' -o yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
[...]
spec:
[...]
  template:
[...]
    spec:
      containers:
      - args:
        - --debug
```

The result should be instead:

```
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
[...]
spec:
[...]
  template:
[...]
    spec:
      containers:
      - args:
        - --other-param
```


### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

### Kubernetes version

$ kubectl version

Server Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"22", GitVersion:"v1.22.10", GitCommit:"eae22ba6238096f5dec1ceb62766e97783f0ba2f", GitTreeState:"clean", BuildDate:"2022-05-24T1

enrichment.problem: The $deleteFromPrimitiveList directive in a strategic merge patch incorrectly retained the specified list items and removed all other elements, contrary to its documented behavior.
enrichment.affected: Any workflow that patches resources (Deployments, Pods, etc.) using strategic merge patches with $deleteFromPrimitiveList, typically via kubectl or client libraries.
enrichment.fix: Updated the strategic merge patch implementation to correctly delete only the items listed under $deleteFromPrimitiveList, leaving the rest of the list untouched.
enrichment.impact: Users can now reliably use $deleteFromPrimitiveList in patches (e.g., via `kubectl patch --type=strategic`) to remove specific entries from primitive list fields such as container args, environment variables, etc., without unintentionally wiping the entire list.

bugOrRegression.description: `kubelet` will ensure /etc/hosts file is mode 0644 regardless of umask.
bugOrRegression.author: luozhiwenn
bugOrRegression.userFacingChange: kubelet will ensure /etc/hosts file is mode 0644 regardless of umask.

enrichment.problem: When kubelet creates the /etc/hosts file for pods, the file's permissions were derived from the process umask. On nodes with a restrictive umask (e.g., 077), the hosts file could be created with permissions such as 0600, making it unreadable by containers and causing DNS resolution failures inside pods.
enrichment.affected: All pods running on nodes where the kubelet process inherits a restrictive umask could experience hosts file permission issues; the fix affects the kubelet component.
enrichment.fix: Kubelet now explicitly sets the /etc/hosts file mode to 0644 after creation, ignoring the current umask. This ensures the file is always world‑readable as expected.
enrichment.impact: Pods can reliably read /etc/hosts for name resolution regardless of the node's umask setting, preventing permission‑related failures in workloads that depend on the hosts file.

issueContext.title: `kubectl expose` fails for apps with same-port, different-protocol
issueContext.body:
Given this deployment:

```
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: multiport
spec:
  replicas: 0
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: multiport
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: multiport
    spec:
      containers:
      - image: k8s.gcr.io/serve_hostname:v1.4
        name: c1
        ports:
        - containerPort: 93
          protocol: TCP
        - containerPort: 93
          protocol: UDP
```

```
$ k expose deploy multiport
The Service "multiport" is invalid: spec.ports[1]: Duplicate value: core.ServicePort{Name:"", Protocol:"UDP", AppProtocol:(*string)(nil), Port:93, TargetPort:intstr.IntOrString{Type:0, IntVal:0, StrVal:""}, NodePort:0}
```

Looking at staging/src/k8s.io/kubectl/pkg/cmd/expose/expose.go, it builds a `protocolsMap` which reduces those 2 ports to one protocol.  It should probably just return a list of {proto, port} or even {proto, port, name} which it extracts from the target.

enrichment.problem: `kubectl expose` failed when a deployment defined multiple container ports with the same numeric port but different protocols (e.g., TCP and UDP), producing a duplicate ServicePort error.
enrichment.affected: Users running `kubectl expose` on Deployments, ReplicaSets, or other workloads that expose the same port number with different protocols (e.g., TCP and UDP).
enrichment.fix: The expose command now generates separate ServicePort entries for each protocol on the same port, allowing a Service to expose both TCP and UDP (or other protocols) on that port.
enrichment.impact: Users can successfully expose multi‑protocol workloads without manual Service YAML edits, fixing a broken workflow for apps that need the same port number for different protocols.

issueContext.title: kubelet: PreStop Hooks can hang termination of a pod beyond pod's termination grace period
issueContext.body:
### What happened?

Termination grace period includes the termination time of prestop hooks and containers in the pod. The total time that the pod terminates should always be < termination grace period seconds.

A misconfigured pod with a preStopHook that hangs indefinitely and pod ignoring SIGTERM can result in the pod taking 2X (double) the termination grace period seconds to terminate.
 

### What did you expect to happen?

The time to terminate the pod should always be <= termination grace period seconds including prestop hook execution time as documented in https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/containers/container-lifecycle-hooks/#hook-handler-execution

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1) Apply the following pod

```
kind: Pod
apiVersion: v1
metadata:
  name: prestop-repro
  labels:
    pod: prestop-repro
spec:
  terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 60
  containers:
  - name: busybox
    lifecycle:
      preStop:
        exec:
          command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "sleep 999999"]
    image: k8s.gcr.io/e2e-test-images/nginx:1.14-2
    command: ["/bin/sh", "-c"]
    args:
      - |
        _term() {
            echo "Caught SIGTERM signal!"
            while true; do sleep 5; done
        }
        trap _term SIGTERM
        while true; do sleep 5; done
```

2) 

```
$ time kubectl delete pod prestop-repro
pod "prestop-repro" deleted

real    2m1.035s
user    0m0.172s
sys     0m0.077s
```

3) Observe it actually took ~120s to terminate the pod not ~60s as would be expected.

### Anything else we need to know?

The kubelet logs for the pod https://gist.github.com/1f76e54b32bc51f1a9525cc8b707f820

```

# pods start terminating at `23:54:37 `

Feb 15 23:54:37 kind-worker kubelet[268]: I0215 23:54:37.470356     268 kubelet.go:1858] "syncTerminatingPod enter" pod="default/prestop-repro" podUID=0f651710-9a93-4424-afe6-646d01698866
Feb 15 23:54:37 kind-worker kubelet[268]: I02

enrichment.problem: When a pod's preStop hook hangs (e.g., sleeps indefinitely) and the container ignores SIGTERM, the pod can exceed its terminationGracePeriodSeconds, taking up to twice the configured time to terminate.
enrichment.affected: Pods with a preStop lifecycle hook that blocks or hangs, especially when the container does not handle SIGTERM.
enrichment.fix: Kubelet now enforces the terminationGracePeriodSeconds for preStop hooks, aborting the hook after the grace period so the pod termination cannot exceed the configured timeout.
enrichment.impact: Pods now reliably terminate within the user‑specified grace period, preventing resource leaks and improving cluster stability for workloads that use preStop hooks.

issueContext.title: CSI volumes left overs are not cleaned up if CSI plugin is attachable
issueContext.body:
### What happened?

1. Create a Deployment or SS that uses a vsphere CSI volumes (for example).
2. Shutdown the node while pod was running.
3. Wait for node to go `NotReady` and pod to switch to `Terminating` state. 
4. Bring back the node up.
5. If the pod migrates to different node (or pod gets deleted), then files/directories inside `/var/lib/kubelet/pods/xxxx` should be cleaned up.

The reason those directories are not being cleaned up is because:

1. The volume types that are attachable, kubelet expects `node-publish-path` to be a mount point during reconstruction. So if node is rebooted then reconstruction fails because `/mount` path is not a mount point.
2. Kubelet tries to "Cleanup" the volume, but CSI driver may be unavailable at this point.
3. As a result volumes are never cleaned up.





### What did you expect to happen?

Expected cleanup to happen properly. 

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

See above

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

### Kubernetes version

master

### Cloud provider

Any

### OS version

Linux

### Install tools

_No response_

### Container runtime (CRI) and version (if applicable)

_No response_

### Related plugins (CNI, CSI, ...) and versions (if applicable)

_No response_

enrichment.problem: When a node goes down and later returns, kubelet fails to clean up the mount point directories of evicted pods using attachable CSI volumes. The cleanup attempts see the node‑publish path as a non‑mount point and the CSI driver may be unavailable, resulting in orphaned pod directories and repeated log messages like “Orphaned pod … error not a directory”.
enrichment.affected: Pods using attachable CSI volumes (e.g., vSphere CSI) on nodes that experience a shutdown/reboot. Kubelet cleanup process was affected.
enrichment.fix: Kubelet’s volume cleanup logic was updated to handle the case where the node‑publish path is not a mount point after node restart and to tolerate temporary CSI driver unavailability. The code now correctly removes the stale volume directories for evicted pods, stopping the orphaned‑pod log spam.
enrichment.impact: Stale volume directories are removed, freeing disk space and eliminating noisy error logs. This ensures proper resource cleanup after node failures, improving cluster stability for workloads that use attachable CSI drivers.

issueContext.title: Last apiserver to shutdown doesn't remove its IP from k8s svc endpoints
issueContext.body:
### What happened?

As part of the apiserver's pre-shutdown sequence, we stop the lease-controller from renewing the apiserver's etcd lease anymore and delete the lease:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/125e38c0872521bec49351415cc9fb624b046659/pkg/controlplane/controller.go#L211-L215

As part of the `RemoveEndpoints` call we expect that after the lease is deleted, the apiserver's IP is also removed from the k8s service endpoints object:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/125e38c0872521bec49351415cc9fb624b046659/pkg/controlplane/reconcilers/lease.go#L315-L321

However, `doReconcile` isn't removing the IP if it's the last remaining one:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/125e38c0872521bec49351415cc9fb624b046659/pkg/controlplane/reconcilers/lease.go#L210-L215

The comment there is assuming that `doReconcile` is always called after renewing the lease, which is incorrect since it can also be called as part of the shutdown workflow.

### What did you expect to happen?

The IP of the apiserver (even though it's the last one remaining) should be removed from k8s svc endpoints on shutdown.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Shutdown the last apiserver of the cluster and you'll see logs like this:

```
I1031 17:34:49.517758      12 controller.go:181] Shutting down kubernetes service endpoint reconciler
E1031 17:34:49.534880      12 controller.go:184] no master IPs were listed in storage, refusing to erase all endpoints for the kubernetes service
```

And the audit logs also confirm that the IP isn't removed from k8s endpoints object.

### Anything else we need to know?

Why is the above an issue?

If the IP isn't removed from the k8s endpoints object, clients (using in-cluster API mode) will try to continue talking/connecting to that instance even after the apiserver is dead. There are at least two issues with this:
- Causes confusing `i/o timeout` and `connection re

enrichment.problem: When the last kube-apiserver instance shuts down gracefully, it fails to remove its IP address from the kubernetes Service endpoints, leaving a stale endpoint that can receive traffic.
enrichment.affected: Clusters performing a graceful shutdown of the final kube-apiserver (e.g., during upgrades or control‑plane scaling) would retain a stale endpoint, affecting clients that query the kubernetes Service.
enrichment.fix: kube-apiserver now always removes its endpoint from the kubernetes Service during graceful shutdown, even when it is the sole or last endpoint.
enrichment.impact: Prevents clients from being directed to a non‑functional apiserver after a shutdown, ensuring the Service endpoint list remains accurate and improving cluster reliability during upgrades or control‑plane scaling.

issueContext.title: `creationTimestamp: null` still causes unnecessary etcd-write with SSA
issueContext.body:
### What happened?

Sending a patch built from a typed client to SSA will force a write to etcd (and bump resourceVersion) since creationTimestamp is serialized to null. This is a follow-up of https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/106388 which doesn't solve the issue properly.

### What did you expect to happen?

Sending a no-op SSA request with creationTimestamp to null shouldn't do anything

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Kubectl apply an object with creationTimestamp null twice and see that it updates the object.
Probably something like this would cause it:
```
for i in "$(seq 1 10); do kubectl apply --server-side=true -f - -o yaml <<EOF
kind: ConfigMap
apiVersion: v1
metadata:
    name: some-configmap
    creationTimestamp: null # This is unfortunately done automatically when using typed client
data:
EOF
done
```

enrichment.problem: `creationTimestamp: null` is serialized into SSA patches, causing a write to etcd and a resourceVersion bump even when the request is a no‑op.
enrichment.affected: Users performing server‑side apply (e.g., `kubectl apply --server-side`) or programs that build SSA patches with typed clients that include `creationTimestamp: null`. All resources are affected because the bug is generic.
enrichment.fix: The serialization logic now omits `creationTimestamp` when its value is null, preventing unnecessary etcd writes during server‑side apply operations.
enrichment.impact: Reduces superfluous etcd traffic, avoids unnecessary resourceVersion increments, and lessens load on the API server and etcd, leading to better performance and fewer spurious watch events.

issueContext.title: `volume.SetVolumeOwnership()` always fails when called for wrapped volume
issueContext.body:
### What happened?

Every time `volume.SetVolumeOwnership(ed)` from `empty_dir.go` is called for a projected volume, it fails with "no such file or directory" error.

The problem comes from the fact that `SetVolumeOwnership()` always calculates the root dir for ownership changes as `mounter.GetPath()` while projected.go explicitly passes another dir as the first arg of `SetUpAt()` call:
```
	if err := wrapped.SetUpAt(dir, mounterArgs); err != nil {
		return err
	}
```
(see https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/96306f144a3c917a97fe27c9ad5dd89e4213f741/pkg/volume/projected/projected.go#L203)

### What did you expect to happen?

`volume.SetVolumeOwnership()` must succeed when a projected volume is created.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Print return value of `volume.SetVolumeOwnership()` when called from `empty_dir.go`:
```
diff --git a/pkg/volume/emptydir/empty_dir.go b/pkg/volume/emptydir/empty_dir.go
index 9ad981c54bd..ce3f7d330fe 100644
--- a/pkg/volume/emptydir/empty_dir.go
+++ b/pkg/volume/emptydir/empty_dir.go
@@ -280,7 +280,10 @@ func (ed *emptyDir) SetUpAt(dir string, mounterArgs volume.MounterArgs) error {
                err = fmt.Errorf("unknown storage medium %q", ed.medium)
        }
 
-       volume.SetVolumeOwnership(ed, mounterArgs.FsGroup, nil /*fsGroupChangePolicy*/, volumeutil.FSGroupCompleteHook(ed.plugin, nil))
+       e := volume.SetVolumeOwnership(ed, mounterArgs.FsGroup, nil /*fsGroupChangePolicy*/, volumeutil.FSGroupCompleteHook(ed.plugin, nil))
+       if e != nil {
+               klog.Infof("ZZZ: SetVolumeOwnership() returned error: %v (dir: %v; ed.GetPath(): %v)", e, dir, ed.GetPath())
+       }
 
        // If setting up the quota fails, just log a message but don't actually error out.
        // We'll use the old du mechanism in this case, at least until we support
```

Start an arbitrary pod, then look at kubelet logs:
```
$ kubectl apply -f fedora.yaml

$

enrichment.problem: SetVolumeOwnership() always failed for projected volumes created inside an emptyDir because it incorrectly used the mounter's path instead of the actual directory passed to SetUpAt, leading to "no such file or directory" errors and inflated error count metrics for emptyDir.
enrichment.affected: Pods that mount an emptyDir volume containing projected sub‑volumes (e.g., ConfigMap or Secret projections) experienced unnecessary error logs and metric noise.
enrichment.fix: The code now passes the correct directory to SetVolumeOwnership (or adjusts the ownership logic) so that projected volumes are set up without error, eliminating the spurious error recordings.
enrichment.impact: Reduces false error spikes in the storage_operation_duration_seconds_count metric, improving observability and preventing misleading alerts for workloads that use emptyDir with projected volumes.

issueContext.title: In-tree vSphere volumes are not detached after KCM restart
issueContext.body:
### What happened?

I am enabling CSI migration on a vSphere cluster. A node was fully drained, all its Pods are deleted, but just before KCM detaches in-tree vSphere volume volumes from it, KCM restarts. A new KCM starts, sees attached volumes in `node.status.volumesAttached` that are not needed by any Pod on the node and calls vSphere in-tree volume plugin `Detach()`.

The in-tree vSphere volume plugin + cloud provider marks the volume as detached right away, without reaching to vCenter API. The volume remains attached forever.

I don't think it's related to CSI migration, IMO a regular node drain + KCM restart at the same time can cause the same issue.

enrichment.problem: When the kube-controller-manager restarts, the in-tree vSphere cloud provider incorrectly skips detaching volumes that are no longer needed, leaving vSphere volumes attached to nodes indefinitely.
enrichment.affected: Clusters that use the in‑tree vSphere cloud provider (and vSphere volume plugin), especially during node drains or when the kube‑controller‑manager restarts.

issueContext.title: PV recycler fails if too many files in top-level directory
issueContext.body:
### What happened?

PV recycler pod fails to remove files if there are `>67567` files in the directory. 

Error in the pod logs:
```
› kl recycler-for-pv-040
2023-04-10T08:17:49.426784970Z /bin/sh: 1: rm: Argument list too long
```

Apparently one hits ARG_MAX due to too long command line. 
https://stackoverflow.com/questions/11289551/argument-list-too-long-error-for-rm-cp-mv-commands



### What did you expect to happen?

PV is recycled successfully

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Claim and NFS pv, create `>67567` files.

```
for i in {001..67568}
do
    echo hello > "/tmp/test/file${i}.txt"
done

# rm /tmp/test/*
-bash: /usr/bin/rm: Argument list too long
```




### Anything else we need to know?

In my testing I have provided my template and replaced the [current command](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/volume/plugins.go#L1068) 

```
test -e /scrub && rm -rf /scrub/..?* /scrub/.[!.]* /scrub/*  && test -z "$(ls -A /scrub)" || exit 1
```

with:
```
test -e /scrub && find /scrub -mindepth 1 -delete && test -z "$(ls -A /scrub)" || exit 1
```

and recycle was successful. 


Maybe I am missing something but the `find -delete` was able to clean up everything (files, folders) and we also need to exclude the `/scrub` folder name.

`debian-base:v2.0.0` already has the `find` command, no changes to image needed.

### Kubernetes version

<details>

```console

Kustomize Version: v4.5.7
Server Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"25", GitVersion:"v1.25.6", GitCommit:"ff2c119726cc1f8926fb0585c74b25921e866a28", GitTreeState:"clean", BuildDate:"2023-01-18T19:15:26Z", GoVersion:"go1.19.5", Compiler:"gc", Platf

enrichment.problem: The persistent volume (PV) recycler pod failed to delete files when the target directory contained more than ~67,000 entries, hitting the system ARG_MAX limit for the `rm` command and producing an “Argument list too long” error.
enrichment.affected: Clusters that rely on the built‑in PV recycler (e.g., NFS or other dynamically provisioned volumes) when the volume’s top‑level directory holds many files. Users experiencing recycle pod failures were unable to reuse the PVs.

issueContext.title: Debugging Profile dosen't work well with PSA
issueContext.body:
### What happened?

I attempted to use `Ephemeral Container`(`kubectl debug`) with `PodSecurity Admission`, but it failed.(related #117130)   
And I found [kubectl debug option](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-cli/1441-kubectl-debug#debugging-profiles) `--profile`, so I tried again with it.  
But it was not work well.  

### What did you expect to happen?

Success to use `Ephemeral Container` with restriction of `PodSecurity Admission`.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

First, create `Namespace` with restriction of `PodSecurity Admission`.  
In this case, set `pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted`.

<details>

`psa-ns.yaml`

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: psa-ns
  labels:
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-version: v1.27
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit: restricted
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit-version: v1.27
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn: restricted
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn-version: v1.27
```

</details>


```concole
$ kubectl apply -f psa-ns.yaml
```

Create the `Pod` that comply with the restrict policy.

<details>

`ubuntu-restricted.yaml`

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  labels:
    run: ubuntu
  name: ubuntu-restricted
  namespace: psa-ns
spec:
  containers:
  - image: ghcr.io/mochizuki875/ubuntu:22.04-runas
    name: ubuntu
    securityContext:
        runAsUser: 1000
        runAsGroup: 1000
        runAsNonRoot: true
        allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
        capabilities:
          drop: 
          - "ALL"
          add:
          - "NET_BIND_SERVICE"
        seccompProfile:

issueContext.title: client-go/kubectl rejects discovery API responses with charset encoding info
issueContext.body:
We are using `client-go` (and `kubectl`) to interact with Kubernetes clusters behind a couple of proxy layers. One of these proxies completes the `Content-Type` headers to include character encoding details.

This was working fine until recently, when client-go/kubectl have started to fail when interacting with the discovery API. It seems that a recent change has made kubectl more restrictive of the content-type that it expects. I suspect that it is related to this commit: https://github.com/kubernetes/client-go/commit/25d5761bfa0603c77cf5efefb14fd2e63a03a773

For example, this is an error from a kubectl command:
```
...
E0422 16:28:02.626222   86629 memcache.go:265] couldn't get current server API group list: Unknown discovery response content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8
I0422 16:28:02.626258   86629 cached_discovery.go:120] skipped caching discovery info due to Unknown discovery response content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8
I0422 16:28:02.626346   86629 shortcut.go:100] Error loading discovery information: Unknown discovery response content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8
...
```

We can of course try to fix it on our end, removing that charset information. However, it is a valid content-type and the way kubectl is handling the content-type there seems like it is relying on implementation details of kube-apiserver (that it does not add metadata to the content-type). I propose to fix this issue in `kubectl`, by properly parsing and handling the content-type.

enrichment.problem: client-go and kubectl reject discovery API responses that include additional parameters (e.g., charset) in the Content-Type header, producing an "Unknown discovery response content-type" error.
enrichment.affected: Users of kubectl or client-go that query the discovery API, particularly when requests pass through proxies that append charset information to the Content‑Type header.
enrichment.fix: The discovery client now tolerates extra content‑type parameters by parsing the media type correctly, allowing responses like "application/json; charset=utf-8" to be accepted.
enrichment.impact: Restores normal operation of kubectl and any client-go based tooling that relies on discovery, especially in environments where proxies add charset information. Prevents unnecessary failures of CLI commands and client‑side discovery caches.

issueContext.title: `ResourceQuota` with "PriortyClass" as its scope is not calculated properly
issueContext.body:
### What happened?

If a Pod is subjected to a `ResourceQuota` with "PriortyClass" as its scope, the quota's calculation is incorrect. See repo steps for more details.

### What did you expect to happen?

`ResourceQuota` with "PriortyClass" as its scope can be calculated at all times.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

- Create a PriorityClass named "p1"
```yaml
apiVersion: scheduling.k8s.io/v1
kind: PriorityClass
metadata:
  name: p1
value: 100
```
- Create a quota with `PriorityClass` as its scope. ⚠️ Note: w/o specifying `PriorityClass`, this issue won't happen
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: quota-p4
spec:
  hard:
    count/pods: "8"
    limits.cpu: "4"
    limits.memory: 2000Gi
    requests.cpu: "4"
    requests.memory: 400Gi
  scopes:
  - PriorityClass <=== Notice this line
  scopeSelector:
    matchExpressions:
    - operator: In
      scopeName: PriorityClass
      values:
      - p1
```
- Create a Job and wait for its completion.
```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: countdown
spec:
  template:
    metadata:
      name: countdown
    spec:
      priorityClassName: p1
      containers:
      - name: counter
        image: alpine
        resources:
          limits:
            cpu: "1"
            memory: 2Gi
          requests:
            cpu: "1"
            memory: 2Gi
        command:
         - "sh"
         - "-c"
         - "for i in 9 8 7 6 5 4 3 2 1 ; do echo $i ; done"
      restartPolicy: Never
```
```
⇒  k get job
NAME        COMPLETIONS   DURATION   AGE
countdown   1/1           7s         8s
```
- Check quota's usage calculation
```
NAME       AGE    REQUEST                                                        LIMIT
quota-p1   2m8s   count/pods: 0/8, requests.cpu: 0/4, requests.memory: 0/400Gi   limits.cpu: 0/4, limits.memory: 0/2000Gi
```
Here `count/pods` is incorrect - it should be `1/8`.

enrichment.problem: ResourceQuota objects that include the PriorityClass scope were counted incorrectly, causing the quota usage to be miscomputed for pods/jobs that specify a priority class.
enrichment.affected: Any cluster using a ResourceQuota with the PriorityClass scope (e.g., jobs or pods that set a priorityClassName) could experience inaccurate quota accounting.
enrichment.fix: The quota calculation logic was corrected to properly account for resources when the "PriorityClass" scope is present, ensuring accurate tracking of hard limits for matching workloads.
enrichment.impact: Clusters that rely on ResourceQuota scoped by PriorityClass will now see correct enforcement of pod and job resource limits, preventing unexpected quota overruns or unnecessary rejections.

issueContext.title: StatefulSet with `podManagementPolicy: Parallel` should create pods in parallel
issueContext.body:
### What would you like to be added?

When `podManagementPolicy: Parallel` is set, StatefulSetController should issue create requests for replicas in batches (similar to how other controllers work, e.g. ReplicaSetController) when creating pods for the first time and scaling up.

### Why is this needed?

Currently even with `Parallel` podManagementPolicy StatefulSet the replicas are still _created_ sequentially, even though they can start to _run_ in any order.

This severely limits pod throughput when working with large StatefulSets (~thousands of replicas). For example, 10 StatefulSets with 5k pods each achieve a total of ~6 pods/s, while 1k StatefulSets with 50 pods each allows for creating ~120 pods/s. 

`Parallel` policy suggests the pods can be created sequentially (https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/kubernetes-api/workload-resources/stateful-set-v1/#StatefulSetSpec): 

>The alternative policy is Parallel which will create pods in parallel to match the desired scale without waiting, and on scale down will delete all pods at once.

Relevant code (`Parallel` policy controls the value of `monotonic`): https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/statefulset/stateful_set_control.go#L424)

enrichment.problem: StatefulSets with podManagementPolicy set to Parallel still created pods sequentially, limiting creation throughput for large numbers of replicas.
enrichment.affected: Users running StatefulSets with podManagementPolicy: Parallel, especially those with many replicas (thousands) or scaling operations.
enrichment.fix: The StatefulSet controller now issues create requests for replicas in parallel batches when podManagementPolicy is Parallel, matching the desired scale without waiting.
enrichment.impact: Significantly faster StatefulSet creation and scaling, allowing higher pod creation rates for large StatefulSets and improving overall cluster scalability.

issueContext.title: APIServices can be deleted at the apiserver startup
issueContext.body:
### What happened?

Initially reported at 1.24.10, but it seems to be present in master as well:

We observe that a part of apiservices objects have been removed by "system:apiserver" right after the kubernetes upgrade.

It looks like there is race between "autoregister controller" [1] deleting apiservices and "crd-autoregister controller" populating a map of desired apiservices, i.e. in logs we see:
```
INFO 2023-05-16T14:21:35.070841Z Starting autoregister controller
INFO 2023-05-16T14:21:35.070858Z Waiting for caches to sync for autoregister controller
INFO 2023-05-16T14:21:35.071116Z Starting crd-autoregister controller
INFO 2023-05-16T14:21:35.071128Z Waiting for caches to sync for crd-autoregister
INFO 2023-05-16T14:21:35.270943Z Caches are synced for autoregister controller
INFO 2023-05-16T14:21:35.471323Z Caches are synced for crd-autoregister
```

The unwanted APIServices delete happened at 14:21:35.438 GMT so between crd-autoregister sync and autoregister controller.

It looks like we attempt to wait with "autoregister controller" for crd-autoregister to initialize here: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/5c1d2d4295f9b4eb12bfbf6429fdf989f2ca8a02/cmd/kube-apiserver/app/aggregator.go#L148-L154

but for some reason we don't enter the if branch.

@liggitt tried adding this diff at HEAD:
```
diff --git a/cmd/kube-apiserver/app/aggregator.go b/cmd/kube-apiserver/app/aggregator.go
index 397c151e66a..8b755ab3179 100644
--- a/cmd/kube-apiserver/app/aggregator.go
+++ b/cmd/kube-apiserver/app/aggregator.go
@@ -148,7 +148,11 @@ func createAggregatorServer(aggregatorConfig *aggregatorapiserver.Config, delega
 			// this prevents the autoregistration controller's initial sync from deleting APIServices for CRDs that still exist.
 			// we only need to do this if CRDs are enabled on this server.  We can't use discovery because we are the source for discovery.
 			if aggregatorConfig.GenericConfig.MergedResourceConfig.ResourceEnabled

enrichment.problem: During kube-apiserver startup, a race condition between the autoregister controller and the crd‑autoregister controller could cause APIService objects for aggregated custom resources to be deleted and then immediately recreated, leading to temporary loss of those APIs.
enrichment.affected: Clusters that use aggregated custom resources (APIService objects) could experience API downtime during apiserver start‑up or upgrade.
enrichment.fix: Adjusted the startup synchronization logic in the apiserver so that the crd‑autoregister controller fully initializes before the autoregister controller attempts to clean up APIService objects, preventing the unintended deletions.

bugOrRegression.description: Improved exponential backoff in Reflector, significantly reducing the load on Kubernetes apiserver in case of throttling of requests.
bugOrRegression.author: marseel

issueContext.title: Improve exponential backoff in reflector
issueContext.body:
Currently, reflector uses two backoff managers: 
https://github.com/kubernetes/client-go/blob/2a5f18df73b70cb85c26a3785b06162f3d513cf5/tools/cache/reflector.go#L223
One is used for initial list call and other for watch call. 

Imagine following scenaraion when k8s apiserver is under very heavy load:
1. At the beginning, reflector spams k8s apiserver (with exponential backoff) with `List` calls until one of them succeeds (due to APF throtling and receiving `429`)
2. Reflector tries to run `Watch` request and uses separate backoffManager - so again spams k8s apiserver with `Watch` requests
3. If Watch does not succeed during Etcd compaction window (2.5 - 5 minutes usually) at some point it will receive `resourceVersionTooOld` and go back to point 1, spamming k8s apiserver again with List calls (because first backoffManager for List got reseted after 2 minutes of retries for Watch requests)

I propose we combine these two backoff managers into one. 
If we combine these two backoffManagers into one, it will work like this:
- At the beginning, reflector spams k8s apiserver (still with exponential backoff) with `List` calls until one of them succeeds
- Tries to make first watch call instantly (as there is no backoff on this path)
- If it fails, it will makre retries every (30, 60)s
- If watch request fails all the times during Etcd compaction window it will go back to List call, but already being throttled with (30, 60)s window. 

/sig scalability

enrichment.problem: Reflector used separate exponential backoff managers for List and Watch requests, causing it to reset the List backoff after Watch retries. Under API server throttling this led to rapid, repeated List and Watch calls, spamming the apiserver and increasing load.
enrichment.affected: All Kubernetes components that use the client-go Reflector for watching resources, such as controller‑manager controllers, the scheduler, kubelet informers, and any custom controllers or operators.
enrichment.fix: Combined the two backoff managers into a single shared backoff. The List call follows exponential backoff as before, but the initial Watch is attempted immediately and then retries on a fixed (30‑60 s) schedule. If Watch continues to fail, subsequent List retries inherit the same backoff, preventing the reset and reducing request bursts.
enrichment.impact: Reduces API server load during throttling, decreases the number of 429 and resourceVersionTooOld errors, and improves reliability of watches and controllers that depend on them, especially in high‑traffic or degraded clusters.

issueContext.title: Indexed Jobs can break with high number of parallelism or completions
issueContext.body:
### What happened?

Currently, the maximum number of completions is MAX_INT32, around 2e9 and the maximum parallelism is 1e5.

When using these values, and assuming a very unlucky case, the field `.status.completedIndexes` can fill up the maximum size for objects in etcd (around 1.5Mi)

/sig apps
/sig scalability

### What did you expect to happen?

An Indexed Job with the maximum number of completions and parallelism to be correctly tracked.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: sample-job
spec:
  completionMode: Indexed
  completions: 2000000000
  parallelism: 100000
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: bad
        image: python
        command:
        - python3
        - -c
        - |
          import os
          import time
          id = int(os.environ.get("JOB_COMPLETION_INDEX"))
          if id > 1000000000 and id % 3 == 0:
            time.sleep(10000)
      restartPolicy: Never
```

In other words, every index multiple of 3 takes too long to terminate.

### Anything else we need to know?

In the example above, the number of characters needed by the `completedIndexes` field is:

`(10+1)*2*1e5`, roughly 2Mi, where:
- 10 is the number of characters for a number
- 1 for the separating character.
- 2 for the consecutive numbers
- 1e5 for the number of "holes" in the `completedIndexes`, based on the parallelism.

### Kubernetes version

1.21 and newer (when IndexedJob was introduced)


### Cloud provider

any

# paste output here

issueContext.title: Pod graceful deletion hangs if the kubelet already rejected that pod at admission time
issueContext.body:
### What happened?

We observed the following series of events:

1) Pod is created with some attributes that later result in the pod being rejected at kubelet admission time
2) The pod is scheduled to a node
3) The pod is gracefully deleted by a controller, i.e. a deletion timestamp is set on the pod
4) The pod is rejected at kubelet admission time
5) The pod never gets deleted and is stuck: despite having the deletion timestamp set. It seems that kubelet does not issue the final force delete for the pod.

This is problematic in many scenarios, but one specific case it was hit was when the pod is backed by a daemonset controller. This issue manifested in way where since the pod never got deleted in step 5 above, the daemonset controller did not create a new pod to run the on the node and thus node was was not running a replica of the daemonset controller pod.

This seems to a be regression in k8s 1.27, I was not able to repro this behavior in 1.26.

### What did you expect to happen?

It is expected at during the series of events above, after the pod is failed at kubelet admission time, since the pod has a deletion timestamp set, the kubelet should forcefully delete the pod. The pod should not hang in deletion forever. 

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Create a 1.27 kind cluster:

```
kind delete cluster


kind_config="$(cat << EOF
kind: Cluster
apiVersion: kind.x-k8s.io/v1alpha4
networking:
  ipFamily: ipv4
nodes:
# the control plane node
- role: control-plane
- role: worker
  kubeadmConfigPatches:
  - |
    kind: JoinConfiguration
    nodeRegistration:
      kubeletExtraArgs:
        v: "4"
        read-only-port: "10255"
EOF
)"

kind create cluster --config <(printf '%s\n' "${kind_config}") --image  kindest/node:v1.27.1@sha256:b7d12ed662b873bd8510879c1846e87c7e676a79fefc93e17b2a52989d3ff42b
```

Stop kubelet
```
$ docker exec -it kind-worker /bin/bash
root@kind-worker:/# sys

enrichment.problem: In Kubernetes 1.27, pods that are rejected by the kubelet admission step but already have a deletionTimestamp (e.g., due to a graceful delete) can get stuck in a deletion state. The kubelet fails to force‑delete these non‑admissible pods, especially after a kubelet restart, leaving the pod forever pending deletion and preventing controllers such as DaemonSet from recreating the pod.
enrichment.affected: Any pod that is rejected at kubelet admission but has been marked for deletion (e.g., pods managed by DaemonSets) and any node where the kubelet restarts while such a pod exists.
enrichment.fix: The kubelet logic was updated to recognize non‑admissible pods with a deletionTimestamp and to forcefully delete them even if the pod was rejected at admission or the kubelet restarted. This ensures the pod is removed and the deletion completes.
enrichment.impact: Stuck pods no longer block controller progress. DaemonSet (and other controllers) can recreate missing pods, restoring expected workload availability and preventing nodes from being left without required replicas.

bugOrRegression.description: Fixed a race condition in `kube-proxy` when using LocalModeNodeCIDR, to avoid dropping Services traffic if the object node is recreated when `kube-proxy` is starting.
bugOrRegression.author: aojea
bugOrRegression.userFacingChange: fix a race condition in kube-proxy when using LocalModeNodeCIDR to avoid dropping Services traffic if the object node is recreated when kube-proxy is starting

issueContext.title: kube-proxy in LocalModeNodeCIDR mode may cache stale Node.PodCIDR if the Node object is recreated
issueContext.body:
### What happened?

If `LocalModeNodeCIDR` is true, kube-proxy reads the `Node.PodCIDR` value and uses it to determine whether or not traffic is local to the Node.

In certain cases (e.g. when kube-proxy runs before the Node information has been completely updated), it is possible for kube-proxy to read and store a stale `PodCIDR` value. This will cause kube-proxy to route traffic incorrectly as the local traffic determination is no longer correct.

Note: PodCIDR is immutable once set but it is possible to delete and recreate the Node object to get into this state. (yes, this can happen)

/sig network

### What did you expect to happen?

kube-proxy should detect this state and reconfigure/restart with the newly updated `PodCIDR`.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Recreate the Node object with a different PodCIDR after kube-proxy has started on the Node.

### Kubernetes version

Impacts all current versions that support `LocalModeNodeCIDR`

### Cloud provider

<details>
Observed for GCE preemptible/spot VMs, but is a generic problem.
</details>

enrichment.problem: When kube-proxy runs with LocalModeNodeCIDR enabled, it can cache a stale Node.PodCIDR if the Node object is deleted and recreated while kube-proxy is starting. The stale CIDR causes kube-proxy to misclassify traffic as non‑local, leading to dropped Service traffic.
enrichment.affected: Nodes running kube-proxy with LocalModeNodeCIDR enabled; Service traffic to pods on those nodes could be dropped if the Node object is recreated during kube-proxy startup.
enrichment.fix: Added synchronization logic in kube-proxy to handle the race condition: it now detects node recreation, re‑reads the updated PodCIDR, and updates its local‑traffic determination, preventing service traffic loss.
enrichment.impact: Ensures that Service traffic continues to flow correctly on nodes using LocalModeNodeCIDR, especially in environments where nodes are frequently recreated (e.g., preemptible/spot VMs). Improves reliability and reduces outages for affected workloads.

issueContext.title: Cronjob status.lastSuccessfulTime not populated by a manually triggered job
issueContext.body:
### What happened?

Given a cronjob created with a scedule of "0 6 * * *" that failed at last run (status.lastSuccessfulTime is now "before" status.lastScheduleTime). 

Then I trigger the cronjob by hand `kubectl create job --from=cronjob/my-cronjob my-cronjob-manual-1234`and this jobs ends successfully. However status.lastSuccessfulTime is not updated, thus making it difficult to monitor failed cronjobs. 

### What did you expect to happen?

status.lastSuccessfulTime should be updated with a timestamp of the succeeded job endTime

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Install the attached files:
```
kubectl apply -f configmap-ok.yaml
kubectl apply -f cronjob_test.yaml
```
Wait until cronjob has actually trigged, test with
```
kubectl get cronjob -o jsonpath='{.items[*].status}' | jq
```
to see that lastScheduleTime and lastSuccessfulTime are populated ok (as expected).
Then apply the fail config-map, now the job will not complete OK:
```
kubectl apply -f configmap-fail.yaml
```
Again wait until cronjob has trigged automatically, observe 
```
kubectl get cronjob -o jsonpath='{.items[*].status}' | jq
```
to see that lastScheduleTime is updated but lastSuccessfulTime is not.

Then apply the "OK" configmap and then create the job by hand:
```
kubectl apply -f configmap-ok.yaml
kubectl create job --from=cronjob/test-cronjob test-cronjob-manual-$(date +%s)
```
when the job has finished and completed ok, observe that lastSuccessfulTime is still not updated.
```
kubectl get cronjob -o jsonpath='{.items[*].status}'
```
Wait until next schedule and observe that the field is now updated.



### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

<details>

```console
$ kubectl version

Client Version: version.

issueContext.title: wait.PollUntilContextTimeout with immediate=true does not invoke condition function at least once
issueContext.body:
### What happened?

Calling wait.PollUntilContextTimeout with immediate=true does not invoke the passed condition function if context has already been cancelled.



### What did you expect to happen?

wait.PollUntilContextTimeout with immediate=true should invoke the passed condition function at least once even if context has already been cancelled as wait.PollUntilContextCancel documentation says:

> If immediate is true, condition will be invoked before waiting and guarantees that condition is invoked at least once, regardless of whether the context has been cancelled.

Note that wait.PollUntilContextTimeout wraps wait.PollUntilContextCancel, so the above should be applied to wait.PollUntilContextTimeout as well.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

```go
package main

import (
        "context"
        "time"

        "k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/wait"
)

func main() {
        err := wait.PollUntilContextTimeout(context.Background(), time.Second, 0, true, func(context.Context) (bool, error) {
                return true, nil
        })
        if err != nil {
                panic(err)
        }
}
```

This program panics because context ctx.Err is checked before invoking the passed function.


### Anything else we need to know?

The deprecated wait.PollImmediateWithContext does not have this kind of issue.
If wait.PollUntilContextTimeout is the replacement of wait.PollImmediateWithContext, it should exhibit the same behavior.

issueContext.title: apiregistration.k8s.io is not available in openapi/v3 endpoint and discovery
issueContext.body:
### What happened?

it is not possible to discover apiregistration.k8s.io in openapi/v3. 

```shell
$ kubectl explain apiservices
error: couldn't find resource for "apiregistration.k8s.io/v1, Resource=apiservices"
```

This was possible to do with v2.

```shell
$ kubectl explain apiservices --output=plaintext-openapiv2
KIND:     APIService
VERSION:  apiregistration.k8s.io/v1
...
```

### What did you expect to happen?

openapi/v3 discovery works for apiregistration.k8s.io 

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

```shell
$ curl -k -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" https://localhost:6443/openapi/v3 | grep apiregistration
```

```shell

issueContext.title: meaning of sync_proxy_rules_iptables_total given MinimizeIPTablesRestore
issueContext.body:
The `sync_proxy_rules_iptables_total` metric is defined as "Number of proxy iptables rules programmed".

In the past, that effectively meant "the total number of rules in iptables that kube-proxy owns". But post-`MinimizeIPTablesRestore`, it now ends up being "the number of iptables rules that changed in the last sync". (FWIW this is only a change for the `nat` half of the metric; currently we always rewrite all `filter` rules, even in a partial sync, so the `filter` half of the metric is still "correct".)

There are arguments for either meaning, but I think the traditional ("total number of rules in iptables that kube-proxy owns") is more useful?

One possibility would be to only set the metric during full syncs, but in that case we might go a very long time without updating it, and it would get out of date.

Another possibility would be that instead of setting that metric from the `iptables-restore` _input_, we could set it from the `iptables-save` _output_. This would mean that it would always lag by (at least) one sync (since it would be set based on the rules we are replacing rather than the rules we are creating) but that would at least be more up-to-date than waiting for the next full resync. (In `largeClusterMode`, it would lag a bit more, only getting updated once every `syncPeriod` (default 30s).)

If we think it's important to have it always be up-to-date then we could try to figure out some way to calculate the right value during a partial update... in that case we'd have to run through the code that currently gets bypassed during a partial update, and have it decide what rules are needed, but not actually try to write them.

/sig network

enrichment.problem: Since Kubernetes 1.27 the kube-proxy metric `sync_proxy_rules_iptables_total` reported only the number of iptables rules that were re‑synced in the last sync (due to MinimizeIPTablesRestore), instead of the total number of iptables rules owned by kube‑proxy. This broke existing monitoring and alerting that expected the historic "total rules" semantics.
enrichment.affected: Clusters using kube-proxy with iptables mode that monitor the `sync_proxy_rules_iptables_total` metric for rule counts, especially those that adopted the MinimizeIPTablesRestore feature.
enrichment.fix: The metric is restored to its original pre‑1.27 behavior: it now again reports the total number of iptables rules managed by kube‑proxy. A new metric `sync_proxy_rules_iptables_last` is added to expose the number of rules changed in the most recent sync.
enrichment.impact: Monitoring, dashboards, and alerting that rely on the total rule count regain correct values, eliminating confusion. The new metric gives operators additional insight into how many rules changed per sync, aiding troubleshooting and capacity planning.

bugOrRegression.description: Declare Job as finished only after removing all Pod finalizers to avoid orphan Pods.
bugOrRegression.author: alculquicondor
bugOrRegression.userFacingChange: Only declare Job as finished after removing all Pod finalizers to avoid orphan Pods

enrichment.problem: Jobs were marked as completed before all Pods' finalizers were removed, leaving orphan Pods that persisted after the Job finished.
enrichment.affected: Users running Jobs where Pods have finalizers; orphan Pods could remain after Job completion.
enrichment.fix: The Job controller now waits until all finalizers are removed from its Pods before marking the Job as finished, ensuring proper Pod cleanup.
enrichment.impact: Prevents leftover Pods that waste resources and cause confusion, improving reliability of Job cleanup for users who use finalizers on Pods.

bugOrRegression.description: Bumped cadvisor version to `v0.47.3`.
bugOrRegression.author: iholder101

enrichment.affected: All clusters running the kubelet will run the newer cAdvisor; workloads are indirectly affected through more stable metric collection and reduced node‑level failures.

enrichment.impact: Improves reliability and accuracy of node-level resource metrics, reduces potential cAdvisor‑related crashes, and brings in upstream security and performance patches for all clusters using the kubelet.

bugOrRegression.description: Fixed a bug where `kubectl port-forward`, when used with a Deployment, could connect to a terminating pod even when a running pod is also available.

bugOrRegression.description: Fixed computing backoff delay when using Job pod failure policy, by including in the backoff delay calculation pod failures ignored from the backoffLimit counter.
bugOrRegression.author: mimowo
bugOrRegression.userFacingChange: Fix computing backoff delay when using Job pod failure policy, by including in the backoff delay calculation pod failures ignored from the backoffLimit counter

issueContext.title: Job: Pod backoff calculation should not depend on failure policy
issueContext.body:
### What happened?

Pod backoff calculation excludes pods that match an `Ignore` rule in the failure policy:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/847f1758748ac357e79094c5e85029a10428e65f/pkg/controller/job/job_controller.go#L1365

This could lead to fast retries, overwhelming the control plane, if most failures match an `Ignore` rule. The semantics of `Ignore` is not to count towards the limit, but the backoff should still be respected.

/sig apps

### What did you expect to happen?

Recreations to be throttled.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create a Job with failure policy that matches every kind of failure.
1. Use a container that always fails

You would observe immediate recreation.

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

### Kubernetes version

1.27+

### Cloud provider

<details>
N/A
</details>


### OS version

<details>

```console
# On Linux:
$ cat /etc/os-release
# paste output here
$ uname -a
# paste output here

# On Windows:
C:\> wmic os get Caption, Version, BuildNumber, OSArchitecture
# paste output here
```

</details>


### Install tools

<details>

</details>


### Container runtime (CRI) and version (if applicable)

<details>

</details>


### Related plugins (CNI, CSI, ...) and versions (if applicable)

<details>

</details>

enrichment.problem: When a Job uses a pod failure policy with an `Ignore` rule, failures that are ignored for the `backoffLimit` counter were also excluded from the backoff delay calculation. This caused pods to be recreated immediately without the expected throttling, potentially flooding the control plane with rapid retries.
enrichment.affected: Jobs that define a pod failure policy with `Ignore` rules (e.g., to ignore certain failure types) were affected because their pod restarts could happen without backoff.
enrichment.fix: The Job controller now includes pod failures that are ignored by the failure policy in the backoff delay calculation, while still not counting them toward the `backoffLimit`. This restores proper backoff behavior for Jobs with failure policies.
enrichment.impact: Jobs that rely on pod failure policies will now respect backoff intervals, preventing fast, unchecked restarts and reducing load on the control plane. Users get the expected retry throttling semantics, improving reliability and stability of batch workloads.

feature.description: Added support for pod `hostNetwork` field selector
feature.author: halfcrazy

enrichment.problem: Before this change, the Kubernetes API did not allow a field selector on the pod spec.hostNetwork field, so users could not directly query or filter pods that were using the host network.
enrichment.affected: Any workflow that needs to identify pods running with hostNetwork enabled (e.g., network troubleshooting, security policies, custom controllers).
enrichment.fix: Added support for the `spec.hostNetwork` field in pod field selectors, enabling API queries like `?fieldSelector=spec.hostNetwork=true`.
enrichment.impact: Operators and developers can now select, list, and watch pods based on their hostNetwork setting, simplifying troubleshooting, policy enforcement, and automation that depends on host network usage.

feature.description: Migrated the certificate controller (within `kube-controller-manager`) to use [contextual logging](https://k8s.io/docs/concepts/cluster-administration/system-logs/#contextual-logging).
feature.author: mengjiao-liu

enrichment.problem: The certificate controller in kube-controller-manager emitted plain logs without structured context, making it difficult for operators to correlate log lines and troubleshoot certificate-related issues.
enrichment.affected: Clusters running the certificate controller (part of kube-controller-manager). Operators troubleshooting certificate issuance or rotation will see more useful log output.
enrichment.fix: The controller was migrated to use the new contextual logging framework, adding structured fields (e.g., component, request ID) to its log messages.
enrichment.impact: Logs from the certificate controller are now richer and easier to filter, search, and correlate, improving observability and debugging without changing runtime behavior.

feature.description: Graduated the `ProbeTerminationGracePeriod` feature gate to GA.
feature.author: rphillips
feature.userFacingChange: Graduate the `ProbeTerminationGracePeriod` feature gate to GA

enrichment.problem: The ProbeTerminationGracePeriod feature was only available behind a feature gate, requiring clusters to explicitly enable it and causing uncertainty about default termination behavior for readiness/liveness probes.
enrichment.affected: Clusters that previously had to enable the ProbeTerminationGracePeriod feature gate manually, as well as any workloads relying on graceful probe termination during pod shutdown.
enrichment.fix: The feature gate has been graduated to GA, making ProbeTerminationGracePeriod always enabled with a default value, removing the need for manual gate activation.
enrichment.impact: Clusters now have deterministic probe termination handling out of the box, simplifying configuration and improving graceful pod shutdown reliability for all workloads.

feature.description: Migrated `pod-security-admission` to use [contextual logging](https://k8s.io/docs/concepts/cluster-administration/system-logs/#contextual-logging).
feature.author: Namanl2001

enrichment.problem: The pod-security-admission admission controller was using generic logging, making it hard to correlate its log entries with specific requests and debug issues.
enrichment.affected: Clusters that enable the pod-security-admission controller. Users relying on logs to audit or debug security admission decisions will see richer, request‑scoped log output.
enrichment.fix: Migrated pod-security-admission to use the new contextual logging framework, attaching request‑level context (such as user, namespace, and pod name) to each log entry.
enrichment.impact: Improves observability and troubleshooting for pod security policy enforcement. Administrators can now quickly find relevant logs for specific admission decisions, reducing mean‑time‑to‑diagnose security‑related problems.

feature.description: Added a new command line argument `--interactive` to kubectl. The new command line argument lets a user confirm deletion requests per resource interactively.
feature.author: ardaguclu

enrichment.problem: kubectl delete commands could remove multiple resources without any user confirmation, leading to accidental mass deletions.
enrichment.affected: All users of kubectl who run delete commands, especially those using scripts or handling many resources at once.
enrichment.fix: Introduces a new `--interactive` flag for kubectl that prompts the user to confirm each resource deletion individually before proceeding.
enrichment.impact: Provides a safety net for operators and developers, reducing the risk of unintended resource loss and improving confidence when running bulk delete operations.

feature.description: Migrated the `EndpointSlice` and `EndpointSliceMirroring` controllers (within `kube-controller-manager`) to use [contextual logging](https://k8s.io/docs/concepts/cluster-administration/system-logs/#contextual-logging).
feature.author: Namanl2001

enrichment.problem: The EndpointSlice and EndpointSliceMirroring controllers emitted logs without contextual information, making it harder for operators to correlate log entries with specific resources or actions.
enrichment.affected: Clusters running the kube-controller-manager, especially those troubleshooting EndpointSlice behavior or monitoring network service health.
enrichment.fix: The controllers in kube-controller-manager were migrated to use the new contextual logging framework, attaching structured context (e.g., namespace, service name, endpoint IDs) to each log line.
enrichment.impact: Improves diagnostic experience for cluster operators and developers by providing richer, searchable logs, reducing time to troubleshoot networking and service‑discovery issues.

feature.description: Allow to monitor client-go DNS resolver latencies via `rest_client_dns_resolution_duration_seconds` Prometheus metric.
feature.author: mfojtik

enrichment.problem: There was no built-in way to observe the latency of DNS lookups performed by the client-go HTTP client, making it difficult to diagnose DNS-related performance issues in components that use client-go.
enrichment.affected: All Kubernetes control-plane components and any workloads that use the client-go library (e.g., kube-apiserver, controller-manager, scheduler, kubectl) previously could not monitor DNS resolution latency.
enrichment.fix: A new Prometheus metric `rest_client_dns_resolution_duration_seconds` is exposed, measuring the duration of DNS resolution for client-go requests.
enrichment.impact: Operators and developers can now monitor and alert on DNS resolver latency from any component that uses client-go, improving troubleshooting and overall cluster observability.

feature.description: kubelet: security of dynamic resource allocation was enhanced by limiting node access to those objects that are needed on the node.
feature.author: pohly

issueContext.title: dynamic resource allocation: use node authorizer to lock down access by kubelet
issueContext.body:
### What would you like to be added?

kubelet should only be able to read ResourceClaims that are needed by a pod that has been scheduled onto the node.

The node authorizer can do that, similar to how volumes are limited.

### Why is this needed?

Better security if a node gets compromised.

enrichment.problem: kubelet could read any ResourceClaim objects, even those not needed for pods scheduled on the node, exposing unnecessary data if a node were compromised.
enrichment.affected: All nodes running kubelet with dynamic resource allocation enabled; pods that use ResourceClaims are impacted because kubelet now restricts claim access.
enrichment.fix: Implemented node authorizer checks so kubelet is only granted read access to ResourceClaims that belong to pods scheduled on that node, limiting its view to required objects.
enrichment.impact: Reduces the attack surface of a compromised node by preventing enumeration of unrelated ResourceClaims, improving cluster security for workloads using dynamic resource allocation.

feature.description: In the course of admitting a single request, the ValidatingAdmissionPolicy plugin will perform no more than one authorization check per unique authorizer expression. All evaluations of identical authorizer expressions will produce the same decision.
feature.author: benluddy

enrichment.problem: The ValidatingAdmissionPolicy admission plugin could perform multiple redundant authorization checks for the same authorizer expression during a single request, leading to unnecessary API server latency and load.
enrichment.affected: Clusters that use the ValidatingAdmissionPolicy feature; any workload whose create/update requests trigger the plugin.
enrichment.fix: The plugin now deduplicates authorizer expressions per request, performing at most one check per unique expression and reusing that decision for all identical evaluations.
enrichment.impact: Reduces API server admission latency and CPU usage, especially in clusters with many policies that reuse the same authorizer expressions, while guaranteeing consistent authorization decisions.

feature.description: [Kube-proxy]: Implemented connection draining for terminating nodes.
feature.author: alexanderConstantinescu
feature.userFacingChange: [Kube-proxy]: implement connection draining for terminating nodes, KEP-3836

enrichment.problem: When a node is terminated (e.g., during upgrades or scale‑down), kube-proxy immediately stops forwarding traffic, causing existing connections to be dropped and leading to brief service outages.
enrichment.affected: Nodes that are being terminated and the pods/services that rely on kube-proxy for traffic routing on those nodes.
enrichment.fix: Kube-proxy now implements connection draining for terminating nodes. It gracefully stops accepting new connections and allows existing connections to finish before fully removing the node from service.
enrichment.impact: Provides smoother node shutdowns, reduces dropped connections, and improves application reliability during upgrades, scaling, or any node termination scenario.

feature.description: Scheduler now waits for handlers to finish syncing before the scheduling cycles start.
feature.author: AxeZhan
feature.userFacingChange: schedular now waits for handlers to finish syncing before the scheduling cycles start.

issueContext.title: Scheduler: Make sure handlers have synced before scheduling
issueContext.body:
### What would you like to be added?

Make sure handlers have finished syncing before the scheduling cycles start.

Ref: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/113763#issuecomment-1472858978

/sig scheduling
/good-first-issue

### Why is this needed?

In a highly used cluster, we don't want to start scheduling pods before all the pods have been loaded into the scheduler cache, or we could end up in a bad state.

enrichment.problem: The scheduler could begin scheduling cycles before its event handlers had finished syncing, meaning the scheduler cache might be missing pods. In heavily used clusters this could lead to pods being scheduled based on incomplete information, resulting in incorrect placement or unmet scheduling constraints.
enrichment.affected: Kubernetes clusters where the scheduler cache may be out‑of‑sync at start‑up or after a resync, potentially causing incorrect pod placement.
enrichment.fix: The scheduler now blocks the start of each scheduling cycle until all registered handlers report that they have completed their initial synchronization, ensuring the cache is fully populated before any pod is considered for placement.
enrichment.impact: Clusters will no longer experience scheduling decisions made on stale or incomplete cache data, improving reliability of pod placement especially in large or high‑throughput environments. No operational changes are required by users.

issueContext.title: Jobs create replacement Pods as soon as a Pod is marked for deletion
issueContext.body:
### What happened?

When a Pod belonging to a Job is deleted, the job controller creates a replacement pod immediately, even if parallelism is set to 1 and backoffLimit is set to 0.

### What did you expect to happen?

This depends on the use case, but some applications fail when there are more than one pod.

For example, tensorflow fails with:

```
 /job:worker/task:4: Duplicate task registration with task_name=/job:worker/replica:0/task:4
```

This applications will benefit from a delayed Pod creation until the original Pod is marked as Failed/Succeeded.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create a Job that takes some time to clean up on SIGTERM. You can use `gcr.io/k8s-staging-perf-tests/sleep` with `-termination-grace-period 1m`
2. Delete the pod.
3. Observe that there are two pods running.

While here we do a manual DELETE, it could come as a result of preemption from kube-scheduler or a Node maintenance event, which could be common.

### Anything else we need to know?

IIUC, the existing behavior is similar to that of ReplicaSets and it's the behavior that Jobs had from the beginning.

A comment from an internal discussion with @erictune:

> This non-locking behavior was chosen when Job was designed.  At that time, there was no completionMode: Indexed.  Without an index, even if we waited for complete termination, the user would still need to do their own locking/coordination process, or ensure idempotence.  So it would just slow down the Job controller with no benefit.  

Also, at that time there was no PodFailurePolicy. If the user sets a rule for FailJob, we might be creating a replacement pod before being able to act on the policy (related to point 3 in https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-apps/3329-retriable-and-non-retriable-failures#marking-pods-as-failed kubernetes/enhancements#3329).

So I propose that we treat this as a bugfix for Jobs (Indexed or NonI

enrichment.problem: When a Pod belonging to a Job is deleted (e.g., via manual delete, preemption, or node maintenance), the Job controller immediately creates a replacement Pod even if the original Pod has not fully terminated. This can lead to multiple concurrent Pods for a Job with parallelism=1, causing errors in applications that require exclusive execution (e.g., TensorFlow duplicate task registration).
enrichment.affected: Jobs with parallelism set to 1 (or limited parallelism) that rely on single active Pod semantics, particularly workloads sensitive to duplicate Pods such as TensorFlow tasks. Also affects any scenario where Pods are deleted by the scheduler or node maintenance.
enrichment.fix: Introduce the PodRecreationPolicy implementation, which by default (or when set) makes the Job controller wait until the existing Pod reaches a fully terminated state (Succeeded/Failed) before creating a new replacement Pod.
enrichment.impact: Prevents duplicate Pods for Jobs that need single-instance semantics, eliminating runtime errors and ensuring correct job completion. Improves reliability for workloads that rely on graceful termination and exclusive pod execution, especially during preemptions or node maintenance.

feature.description: The Kubernetes apiserver now emits a warning message for Pods with a null labelSelector in podAffinity or topologySpreadConstraints. The null labelSelector means "match none". Using it in podAffinity or topologySpreadConstraint could lead to unintended behavior.
feature.author: sanposhiho

issueContext.title: add the warning in the Pod creation with empty label selector in the pod affinity and topology spread
issueContext.body:
### What would you like to be added?

Currently, when the Label Selector in the Pod Affinity is empty, no objects will be match.
That means if it's in a required PodAffinity, the Pod will never be schedulable. And if it's in a required PodAntiAffinity, that PodAntiAffinity will be no-op. 

So, I'm thinking PodAffinity with empty Label Selector is very likely mistake. It'd be good if we could notice it for users.

### Why is this needed?

To prevent such a misconfiguration.
Probably, we cannot filter out such a Pod creation in the validation for a backward compatibility.

/assign
/sig scheduling

enrichment.problem: Pods created with a null (empty) labelSelector in podAffinity or topologySpreadConstraints match no pods, causing required affinities to make the pod unschedulable and required anti‑affinities to become no‑ops. This silent misconfiguration can lead to unexpected scheduling behavior.
enrichment.affected: Any workload that creates Pods with empty label selectors in podAffinity or topologySpreadConstraints, potentially causing pods to never become schedulable.
enrichment.fix: The kube‑apiserver now emits a warning during Pod creation when a null labelSelector is detected in podAffinity or topologySpreadConstraints, alerting users to the likely mistake.
enrichment.impact: Users are warned about a configuration that would otherwise silently prevent pods from being scheduled or make anti‑affinity rules ineffective, reducing debugging time and preventing workload downtime caused by unschedulable pods.

feature.description: Added '--concurrent-job-syncs' flag for `kube-controller-manager` to set the number of job controller workers.
feature.author: tosi3k
feature.userFacingChange: Add '--concurrent-job-syncs' flag for kube-controller-manager to set the number of job controller workers

issueContext.title: Allow ConcurrentJobSyncs to be set for kube-controller-manager
issueContext.body:
**What would you like to be added**:
The ability to set `ConcurrentJobSyncs` for the kube-controller-manager at runtime.  It looks like the option exists in the code, but a mechanism is not available to set it via kops.  If I understand the code correctly, a flag needs to be added in order to be able to set the value using kops.

**Why is this needed**:
We want to shift a lot of our batch processing jobs from running directly on our CI servers to running as jobs on Kubernetes.  Unfortunately if too many jobs are launched on kubernetes, they begin to back up.  We've noticed up to a 10 minute delay between when the logs indicate that a job has finished and when the kubernetes API actually reflects the same on our small ~30 node cluster.

enrichment.problem: The number of concurrent job controller workers (ConcurrentJobSyncs) could not be configured at runtime, causing job status updates to lag and job backlogs on clusters with many jobs.
enrichment.affected: Clusters running many Job resources, particularly on small to medium sized clusters where the default concurrency limit causes delays.
enrichment.fix: Introduces a new '--concurrent-job-syncs' flag to kube-controller-manager, allowing operators to set the number of job controller workers via the command line or configuration tools.
enrichment.impact: Operators can tune job controller concurrency to match cluster size and workload volume, reducing job completion latency and preventing backlogs, especially on smaller clusters handling large numbers of batch jobs.

enrichment.impact: Operators can now track etcd request traffic and error rates, set alerts, and more quickly identify storage‑related problems, improving cluster observability and reliability.
