feature.userFacingChange: Rename PodHasNetwork to PodReadyToStartContainers

enrichment.problem: The pod condition `PodHasNetwork` had an ambiguous name, leading to confusion for developers and tests that reference it.
enrichment.affected: Users and automation that query or watch the `PodHasNetwork` condition (e.g., custom controllers, CI tests) need to update references to the new name.
enrichment.fix: Renamed the condition to `PodReadyToStartContainers` across the codebase, documentation, and tests, following KEP 3085.
enrichment.impact: Provides a clearer, more accurate description of the pod's readiness state before containers start, reducing misunderstandings and simplifying code that inspects pod conditions. No runtime behavior change.

feature.description: kube-proxy handles Terminating EndpointSlices conditions and enables zero downtime deployments for Services with ExternalTrafficPolicy=Local author: @andrewsykim
feature.author: aojea

enrichment.problem: During rolling updates, kube-proxy did not exclude endpoints marked as Terminating in EndpointSlices, causing traffic to be sent to pods that were shutting down. This resulted in brief service interruptions for Services with ExternalTrafficPolicy=Local.
enrichment.affected: Clusters that use Services with ExternalTrafficPolicy=Local, especially during rolling updates or pod termination, across all platforms (Linux and Windows).
enrichment.fix: kube-proxy now respects the Terminating condition on EndpointSlices and stops routing traffic to those endpoints. This enables continuous traffic flow and zero‑downtime deployments for Services using ExternalTrafficPolicy=Local.
enrichment.impact: Users can perform rolling updates of workloads behind a Local external traffic service without experiencing downtime, improving reliability for edge, ingress, and load‑balanced applications.

feature.description: Kubernetes is now built with Go `1.20.4`.

only giving a weighted average of the two sync types together.

kube-proxy in iptables mode now has separate `sync_full_proxy_rules_duration_seconds`
and `sync_partial_proxy_rules_duration_seconds` (in addition to the existing
`sync_proxy_rules_duration_seconds`), to give better information about how long

feature.description:

"plugin_evaluation_total" metric supports prescore/score extension point.

issueContext.title: metrics to see which plugins affect to scheduler's decisions in Filter/Score phase
issueContext.body:
### What would you like to be added?

metrics to see more details related to scheduler's decisions in Filter phase


### Why is this needed?

In some cases (e.g. new feature is added in scheduler and want to see if it works or not), we may want to see which filter plugin affected Pod's scheduling results and it would be nice if we can observe that in metrics.

Ref: https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/pull/3338#discussion_r890411398

/cc @alculquicondor 
/sig scheduling

enrichment.problem: The plugin_evaluation_total metric was incremented for prescore/score plugins even when those plugins took no action on a pod, leading to misleading observability data about which plugins influenced scheduling decisions.
enrichment.affected: Users relying on scheduler observability metrics (e.g., cluster admins, developers debugging scheduling) saw inflated counts for plugins that did nothing, obscuring true plugin influence.
enrichment.fix: The metric is updated to support the prescore/score extension point and is only incremented when a prescore or score plugin actually processes the incoming pod.
enrichment.impact: Provides accurate metrics for scheduler plugin activity, enabling operators and developers to reliably gauge plugin impact and troubleshoot scheduling behavior.

feature.description: `RetroactiveDefaultStorageClass` feature made stable and enabled by default.

feature.userFacingChange: RetroactiveDefaultStorageClass feature is stable and enabled by default.

enrichment.affected: Clusters with PersistentVolumeClaims that were created before a default StorageClass was defined; administrators who had to manually patch those PVCs.
enrichment.fix: The RetroactiveDefaultStorageClass feature is now GA and enabled by default, causing the controller-manager to retroactively assign the default storage class to existing PVCs that lack a storageClassName.

issueContext.title: kubectl wait on arbitrary jsonpath with unknown value
issueContext.body:
### What would you like to be added?

#83094 describes the `kubectl wait` functionality that allows to wait for a JSONPath expression condition to match a value. For example, the following command waits for a pod with the name `busybox1` reaching "Running" phase:

```bash
kubectl wait pod/busybox1 --for=jsonpath='{.status.phase}'=Running
```

The proposal is to extend the syntax of the command by supporting _any non-empty_ values. The extended syntax will look like the following:

```terminal
jsonpath='{JSONPath expression}'[=value]
```

In the new syntax if the `=value` is provided, the behavior will be, as today, to return when the JSONPath expression matches the value. If `=value` is omitted, the behavior will be to return when the JSONPath expression exists and has _any non-empty_  value.



### Why is this needed?

Unfortunately, the use of current syntax of the JSONPath conditions is limited because it is not always possible to know in advance the value that the JSONPath expression will get. For example, if we would like to wait for a LoadBalancer service with the name `loadbalancer1` to get IP "10.0.0.1", we will run the following command:

```bash
kubectl wait service/loadbalancer1 --for=jsonpath='{.status.loadBalancer.ingress[].ip}'="10.0.0.1"
```

However, there is no guarantee that the service will get this IP. It can get any other. So, if we want to wait until the LoadBalancer service will get an IP, any IP, we cannot use `kubectl wait` command. Like this, we cannot wait for annotations and labels that are dynamically assigned when their value can vary.

Today DevOps engineers are forced to compose scripts where they implement the waiting logic by calling `kubectl get` in loops (e.g. [this question][1] on Stackoverflow).

[1]: https://stackoverflow.com/questions/66114851/kubectl-wait-for-service-to-get-external-ip

enrichment.problem: kubectl wait could only match a specific value for a JSONPath expression, making it impossible to wait for the presence of any value when the exact result is unknown (e.g., waiting for a LoadBalancer service to obtain any IP).
enrichment.affected: Anyone using kubectl wait with JSONPath conditions, especially when the target value is unpredictable (e.g., LoadBalancer services, dynamic status fields).
enrichment.fix: The JSONPath condition syntax now makes the '=value' part optional. When omitted (e.g., --for=jsonpath='{.status.loadBalancer.ingress[].ip}'), the wait succeeds as soon as the expression returns any non‑empty JSON value (object or literal).
enrichment.impact: Users can now reliably wait for resources to acquire any value without knowing the exact result beforehand, simplifying scripts and reducing the need for custom polling loops.

feature.description: kube-controller-manager: the dynamic resource controller steps in when a pod got created such that the scheduler ignores it (i.e. spec.nodeName is set) and then takes care of triggering delayed resource claim allocation and/or reserving a claim for the pod.
feature.author: pohly

issueContext.title: Scheduling Pods with dynamic resources and using the Pod `.spec.nodeName` field fails
issueContext.body:
### What happened?

The combination of using the Pod spec nodeName field with the `DynamicResources` scheduler plugin (currently feature-gated) doesn't work. No surprise really as the nodeName field effective bypasses the `DynamicResources` scheduler plugin running, and something rather clever would need to be invented to make things to work. But this is still a bit of a regression compared to the old device plugin model which doesn't have a similar limitation.  @pohly as the author of the dynamic resources feature can explain what could maybe be created to fix this.

Granted, forcing scheduling even with a device plugin resource may or may not succeed at the node level depending on the availability of said plugin resources at the node, but with dynamic resources the failure seems to be currently guaranteed.

The use-case for this is such that the Kubernetes scheduler is effectively being preceded by some other scheduler which runs earlier (say, some HPC framework) which is giving the Pods the node names and somehow knows that there will be enough resources, and then the workloads ought to land in the specified node and the container related work is then handled normally from there on. So basically Kubernetes wouldn't do much in terms of scheduling, but takes over from there.

### What did you expect to happen?

TBH I expected it to fail and it did. The resource claims won't work, since the scheduler plugin isn't getting a chance to do its thing.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Just use DRA with Pod spec nodeName field, one needs a DRA driver obviously.

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

### Kubernetes version

<details>
Working with dynamic-resource-allocation branch from @pohly which recently got merged to the coming 1.26 release

```console
$ kubectl version
Client Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"26", GitVersion:"v1.26.0", GitCommit:"5932fc8c", GitTreeState:"clean", BuildDate:"2022-11-15T12

enrichment.problem: Pods that set `.spec.nodeName` bypass the DynamicResources scheduler plugin, causing the plugin to never run and preventing delayed resource claim allocation or reservation for those pods.
enrichment.affected: Users employing the DynamicResources scheduler plugin (feature‑gated) together with the `.spec.nodeName` field, typically in custom or external scheduling scenarios.
enrichment.fix: The kube‑controller‑manager’s dynamic resource controller now detects pods that were created with a nodeName (i.e., ignored by the scheduler) and triggers the delayed resource claim allocation or reservation for them.
enrichment.impact: Workloads that rely on an external scheduler to pre‑select a node—such as HPC frameworks using dynamic resources—can now have their resource claims allocated correctly, restoring expected functionality that was lost after the regression.

feature.author: carlory
feature.userFacingChange: move non-graceful node shutdown to GA.

enrichment.problem: Previously, handling of non‑graceful node shutdowns (e.g., power loss) was only available as an alpha/beta feature, requiring users to manually enable it. Without it, pods and attached storage could be left in an inconsistent state, risking data loss or prolonged recovery time.

feature.userFacingChange: Add ConsistentListFromCache feature gate that allows apiserver to serve consistent lists from cache

feature.description:
Action required for the custom scheduler plugin developers. 
Here's the breaking change in `EnqueueExtension` in the scheduling framework. 
The `EventsToRegister` in `EnqueueExtension` changed the return value from `ClusterEvent` to `ClusterEventWithHint`. `ClusterEventWithHint` allows each plugin to filter out more useless events via the callback function named `QueueingHintFn`.
When the scheduling queue receives a cluster event, before moving each Pod from unschedulable pod pool to activeQ/backoffQ, it will call QueueingHintFn of plugins that rejected each Pod in the previous scheduling cycle.
Depending on the value returned from QueueingHintFn, the scheduling queue changes how it queues each Pod:
- if more than one QueueingHintFn returns QueueImmediately, it queues Pod to activeQ.
- If no QueueingHintFn returns QueueImmediately and more than one plugin returns QueueAfterBackoff, it queues Pod to backoffQ if Pod is backing off, or to activeQ if Pod's backoff has already finished.
- If all QueueingHintFn return QueueSkip, it puts this pod back to the unschedulable pod pool

Having appropriate QueueingHintFn contributes to reducing useless retries and thus improves the overall scheduler's performance.

**How can I migrate?**

For backward compatibility, nil `QueueingHintFn` is treated as always returning QueueAfterBackoff. 
So, if you want to just keep the existing behavior, you can register `ClusterEventWithHint` with no `QueueingHintFn` in it. 
But, registering appropriate `QueueingHintFn` is, of course, better from a scheduling performance perspective.

enrichment.problem: The scheduling framework API changed: EnqueueExtension.EventsToRegister now returns ClusterEventWithHint instead of ClusterEvent. Plugins that implement custom scheduler plugins must update their code to use the new type and optionally provide a QueueingHintFn, otherwise compilation will fail.
enrichment.affected: Developers of custom kube-scheduler plugins that implement EnqueueExtension. Their plugins will fail to compile until they migrate to the new ClusterEventWithHint API.
enrichment.fix: Update custom scheduler plugins to register ClusterEventWithHint objects. If you want the previous behavior, omit QueueingHintFn (nil) which defaults to QueueAfterBackoff. For better performance, implement QueueingHintFn to return QueueImmediately, QueueAfterBackoff, or QueueSkip as appropriate.
enrichment.impact: Ensures that scheduler plugins can filter out unnecessary cluster events, reducing useless pod retries and improving scheduler throughput. Plugins must be rebuilt with the new API to avoid compile errors.

feature.description:

feature.author: utam0k
feature.userFacingChange:
The scheduler skips the PodTopologySpread Score plugin when nothing to do with the Pod.
It will affect some metrics values related to the PodTopologySpread Score plugin.

enrichment.problem: The scheduler always invoked the PodTopologySpread Score plugin even for pods that did not have any topology spread constraints, causing unnecessary processing and skewing related metrics.

feature.description: Enabled use of pods with volumes and user namespaces. The feature gate was renamed from `UserNamespacesStatelessPodsSupport` to `UserNamespacesSupport`.
feature.author: giuseppe
feature.userFacingChange: Now it is possible to use pods with volumes and user namespaces.  The feature gate was renamed from UserNamespacesStatelessPodsSupport to UserNamespacesSupport

enrichment.problem: Pods running with user namespaces could not use volumes, limiting their ability to store data and restricting workloads that need both user namespace isolation and persistent storage.
enrichment.affected: Any cluster that enables the UserNamespacesSupport feature gate and runs pods with both user namespaces and volume mounts. Previously affected workloads could only run stateless pods.
enrichment.fix: The kubelet and API server now allow pods with user namespaces to attach volumes. The feature gate has been renamed from UserNamespacesStatelessPodsSupport to UserNamespacesSupport to reflect the broader capability.
enrichment.impact: Users can now run stateful workloads (e.g., databases, log collectors) in isolated user namespaces, improving security isolation without sacrificing storage needs. This expands the applicability of user namespaces for production workloads.

feature.description:
Added full cgroup v2 swap support for both `Limited` and `Unlimited` swap.

When `LimitedSwap` is enabled the swap limit would be automatically calculated for
Burstable QoS pods. For Best-Effort/Guaranteed QoS pods, swap would be disabled.

Containers with memory requests equal to their memory limits also won't have
swap access, and it is a way to opt-out of swap for a single container.

The formula for the swap limit for Burstable QoS pods is:
`(<memory-request>/<node-memory-capacity>)*<node-swap-capacity>`.

Support for `cgroup v1` is removed.
feature.author: iholder101
kepLinks: https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/blob/master/keps/sig-node/2400-node-swap/README.md#steps-to-calculate-swap-limit), the swap limit is being automatically calculated for Burstable QoS pods. As written in the KEP, the fomula is: `(<container-request>/<node-memory-capacity>)*<swap-size>)`. On my system, I have approximately 400Gi of total memory and a swap size of approximately 40Gi. Therefore, the swap limit needs to be approximately `(0.5Gi/400Gi)*40Gi == 0.5Gi`.
feature.userFacingChange:
Add full cgroup v2 swap support for both Limited and Unlimited swap.

When LimitedSwap is enabled the swap limit would be automatically calculated for
Burstable QoS pods. For Best-Effort / Guaranteed QoS pods, swap would be disabled.

Containers with memory requests equal to their memory limits also won't have
swap access, and it is a way to opt-out of swap for a single container.

The formula for the swap limit for Burstable QoS pods is:
`(<memory-request>/<node-memory-capacity>)*<node-swap-capacity>`.

Support for cgroup v1 is removed.

enrichment.problem: Kubernetes did not provide swap support on cgroup v2 and only had limited handling for swap under cgroup v1. Swap limits were not automatically calculated for Burstable QoS pods, and there was no way to opt‑out per container. Support for the older cgroup v1 was also being removed, which could break clusters still using it.
enrichment.affected: Clusters that use cgroup v2 on their nodes; Burstable QoS pods now receive an automatically calculated swap limit; Best‑Effort and Guaranteed pods have swap disabled; containers with request = limit can opt out of swap; users running on cgroup v1 lose swap support and must upgrade.
enrichment.fix: Implemented full swap support for cgroup v2, adding both LimitedSwap and UnlimitedSwap modes. When LimitedSwap is enabled, the kubelet automatically calculates a swap limit for Burstable QoS pods using the formula (memory‑request / node‑memory‑capacity) * node‑swap‑capacity. Swap is disabled for Best‑Effort and Guaranteed QoS pods, and for containers whose memory request equals their limit (providing an opt‑out mechanism). Deprecated cgroup v1 code was removed.
enrichment.impact: Nodes running with cgroup v2 can now safely use swap, improving workload stability under memory pressure and giving predictable swap limits for Burstable pods. Clusters still on cgroup v1 lose swap support and must migrate to cgroup v2 to retain swap functionality.

feature.description:
With the `KubeletCgroupDriverFromCRI` feature gate enabled and sufficiently new version of a container
runtime, kubelet automatically detects the cgroup driver config from the container runtime, eliminating
the need to specify the `cgroupDriver` configuration option (or `--cgroup-driver` flag) of kubelet.
feature.author: marquiz
feature.userFacingChange:
With the KubeletCgroupDriverFromCRI feature gate enabled and sufficiently new version of a container
runtime, kubelet automatically detects the cgroup driver config from the container runtime, eliminating
the need to specify the `cgroupDriver` configuration option (or --cgroup-driver` flag) of kubelet.

enrichment.problem: Kubelet required the cgroup driver to be manually configured via the cgroupDriver setting or --cgroup-driver flag, which could lead to mismatches with the container runtime's driver and added operational overhead.
enrichment.affected: Clusters running kubelet with a CRI‑compatible container runtime that previously had to set the cgroupDriver flag manually.
enrichment.fix: When the KubeletCgroupDriverFromCRI feature gate is enabled and the container runtime version supports it, kubelet automatically detects and adopts the cgroup driver used by the runtime, removing the need for manual configuration.
enrichment.impact: Simplifies kubelet setup and prevents driver mismatch errors, making cluster upgrades and node provisioning easier and more reliable.

feature.description: Added handling for pods in podgc for `PodReplacementPolicy` or `PodDisruption`.
feature.author: kannon92
feature.userFacingChange: Add handling for pods in podgc for PodReplacementPolicy or PodDisruption

enrichment.problem: The pod garbage collector could delete pods that were marked with a PodReplacementPolicy or were in the middle of a PodDisruption, causing premature removal of pods that should be retained for replacement or orderly disruption.
enrichment.affected: Any workload that uses the PodReplacementPolicy feature or relies on PodDisruption (e.g., via PodDisruptionBudgets) could have had its pods incorrectly garbage‑collected.
enrichment.fix: PodGC now checks for the presence of a PodReplacementPolicy or an ongoing PodDisruption before considering a pod for garbage collection, ensuring such pods are preserved until they are truly eligible for deletion.
enrichment.impact: Prevents unexpected pod deletions that could disrupt workloads relying on replacement policies or pod disruption budgets, improving stability and correctness of termination handling.

feature.description: Updated cAdvisor to `v0.47.2` and fixed metrics in `cri-o` when a container restarts.
feature.author: harche
feature.userFacingChange: Updated cAdvisor to v0.47.2 - Fix metrics in cri-o when a container restarts

enrichment.problem: cAdvisor reported incorrect container metrics for CRI-O when a container was restarted, leading to inaccurate monitoring data.
enrichment.affected: Nodes running the CRI-O runtime and kubelet (which embeds cAdvisor). Container restarts previously produced stale or missing metric values.
enrichment.fix: cAdvisor was upgraded to v0.47.2, which includes fixes that correctly reset and report metrics after a CRI-O container restart.
enrichment.impact: Users of the CRI-O runtime now see accurate CPU, memory, and other resource metrics for containers that restart, improving reliability of dashboards and alerting.

feature.description: New CEL Library functions to support Kubernetes Quantities.
feature.author: alexzielenski

enrichment.problem: CEL expressions in Kubernetes lacked functions to parse and manipulate Quantity values, limiting the ability to write expressive validation and policy rules involving resource quantities.
enrichment.affected: Users writing CEL expressions for admission control, policies, or custom resources that need to handle resource quantities.
enrichment.fix: Introduced new CEL library functions that understand and operate on Kubernetes Quantity types, enabling parsing, comparison, and arithmetic on quantities within CEL expressions.
enrichment.impact: Allows developers and cluster operators to write richer AdmissionPolicy, ValidatingWebhook, and other CEL‑based rules that involve CPU, memory, and other resource quantities, improving validation accuracy and reducing custom code.

feature.description: CEL authorizer checks no longer raise runtime errors. Calls to "check" will always return a decision object and the authorization error (if any) can be accessed within expressions using the new decision methods "errored" and "error".
feature.author: benluddy

enrichment.problem: Calls to the CEL authorizer's `check` function could raise runtime errors, causing panics and potentially disrupting API server operation.
enrichment.affected: Clusters using CEL-based authorization policies (e.g., via the API server) could experience crashes or denial of service when authorizer checks errored.
enrichment.fix: The authorizer now always returns a decision object. Errors are captured in the decision and can be inspected within CEL expressions via the new `errored` and `error` methods.
enrichment.impact: Prevents unexpected API server crashes due to authorizer runtime errors and enables policies to handle authorization errors gracefully.

feature.description: Added `--concurrency` flag to configure the concurrency of `kubectl diff` execution, defaults to 1.
feature.author: brancz
feature.userFacingChange: Add `--concurrency` flag to configure the concurrency of `kubectl diff` execution, defaults to 1

enrichment.problem: kubectl diff executed resources sequentially, offering no way to control parallelism, which could lead to slower diff operations on large numbers of resources.
enrichment.affected: Any user running `kubectl diff`, especially those diffing many resources at once.
enrichment.fix: Introduces a new `--concurrency` flag for `kubectl diff` that lets users set the number of concurrent diff executions. The default remains 1 to preserve existing behavior.
enrichment.impact: Users can now speed up diff operations by running them in parallel, reducing wait times for large manifests while still being able to limit concurrency for resource‑constrained environments.

feature.description: Replaced `apiserver_storage_db_total_size_in_bytes` with `apiserver_storage_size_bytes` metric.
feature.author: serathius
feature.userFacingChange: Replace `apiserver_storage_db_total_size_in_bytes` with `apiserver_storage_size_bytes` metric

enrichment.problem: The apiserver metric `apiserver_storage_db_total_size_in_bytes` was removed, breaking existing monitoring configurations that reference it.
enrichment.affected: Monitoring setups and alerting rules that scrape `apiserver_storage_db_total_size_in_bytes` from the kube-apiserver.
enrichment.fix: The metric is replaced with `apiserver_storage_size_bytes`, which provides the same storage size information under a new name.
enrichment.impact: Users must update dashboards, alerts, and any tooling that queries the old metric name to continue receiving storage size data from the API server.

feature.description: `TopologyManagerPolicyOptions` feature-flag is promoted to beta and enabled by default.
feature.author: PiotrProkop
feature.userFacingChange: TopologyManagerPolicyOptions feature-flag is promoted to beta and enabled by default.

enrichment.problem: TopologyManagerPolicyOptions was an alpha feature and disabled by default, so clusters could not use the new topology manager policy options without manually enabling the feature gate.
enrichment.affected: Kubelet on all nodes that run the topology manager; any workloads that rely on NUMA‑aware pod placement.
enrichment.fix: The TopologyManagerPolicyOptions feature gate is promoted to beta and is now enabled by default, making the policy options available out‑of‑the‑box.
enrichment.impact: Clusters can immediately take advantage of richer topology manager policies for NUMA‑aware pod placement and resource allocation without extra configuration, improving performance and predictability of workloads on NUMA nodes.

feature.description: When a pod is done or not going to run, then `ResourceClaims` for it can be reused by other pods or deleted.
feature.author: pohly
feature.userFacingChange: When a pod is done or not going to run, then ResourceClaims for it can be reused by other pods or deleted.

issueContext.title: dynamic resource allocation: delete generated ResourceClaims
issueContext.body:
At the moment, dynamic resource allocation relies on the garbage collector to delete a ResourceClaim that was created from a template for a specific pod. But that garbage collection only happens when the pod actually gets deleted.

That means that for pods that linger after having failed or completed (manually created test pods, jobs), resources remain allocated for extended periods of time although they are not needed anymore and could be reused for other claims.

The solution outlined in the KEP is to make the `resourceclaim` controller also responsible for deleting ResourceClaims when it detects that a pod no longer needs the claim.

enrichment.problem: ResourceClaims created for dynamically allocated resources were only garbage-collected when the pod object was deleted. Pods that completed, failed, or were never scheduled left their ResourceClaims lingering, causing resource leakage and preventing reuse of those claims.
enrichment.affected: Pods that use dynamic ResourceClaims (e.g., Jobs, test pods, or any workload with a ResourceClaimTemplate) were affected because their claims were not cleaned up after the pod finished or failed.
enrichment.fix: The resourceclaim controller now detects when a pod is finished, failed, or will not run and either deletes the associated ResourceClaim or marks it reusable for other pods, enabling automatic reclamation of the resources.
enrichment.impact: Clusters no longer retain unused ResourceClaims, freeing up allocated resources and allowing other workloads to claim them. This prevents unnecessary resource consumption, reduces the chance of resource exhaustion, and improves overall scheduling efficiency for workloads that use dynamic resource allocation.

feature.description: `kubeadm`: added the `--allow-experimental-api` flag to "kubeadm config migrate/validate" commands. It can be used to migrate or validate WIP/experimental APIs in the future.
feature.author: neolit123
feature.userFacingChange: kubeadm: add the --allow-experimental-api flag to "kubeadm config migrate/validate" commands. It can be used to migrate or validate WIP / experimental APIs in the future.

enrichment.problem: kubeadm config migrate and validate commands could not process work-in-progress or experimental API versions, preventing administrators from migrating or validating configurations that used such APIs.
enrichment.affected: Users running `kubeadm config migrate` or `kubeadm config validate` on clusters with experimental or work‑in‑progress API objects in their configuration files.
enrichment.fix: Introduced a new `--allow-experimental-api` flag for both `kubeadm config migrate` and `kubeadm config validate`. When provided, the commands accept and handle experimental/WIP API versions.
enrichment.impact: Cluster administrators can now safely migrate or validate configurations that include experimental APIs, reducing friction when preparing for upcoming API changes and avoiding unnecessary migration failures.

feature.description:
`kubeadm`: generate CA certificates with a start time that is offset 5
minutes in the past relative to the current system time to workaround cases of
clock desync.
feature.author: champtar
feature.userFacingChange:
kubeadm: generate CA certificates with a start time that is offset 5 minutes in the past relative to the current system time to workaround cases of clock desync.
client-go: allow to set NotBefore in NewSelfSignedCACert()

enrichment.problem: When system clocks are out of sync, kubeadm-generated CA certificates could have a NotBefore timestamp in the future, causing the certificates to be considered invalid and breaking cluster initialization or join operations.
enrichment.affected: Users initializing or joining clusters with kubeadm on nodes where the system clock is drifted, affecting all components that rely on the generated CA (API server, controller‑manager, scheduler, kubelet, etc.).
enrichment.fix: kubeadm now backdates the CA certificate's NotBefore field by 5 minutes relative to the current system time. client-go adds support to explicitly set NotBefore in NewSelfSignedCACert(), enabling this workaround.
enrichment.impact: Cluster bootstrapping with kubeadm becomes reliable even in environments with slight clock skew, reducing certificate‑related failures and the need for manual time synchronization.

feature.description: Dynamic resource allocation: when a claim uses "wait for first consumer" allocation (the default), then it will now get deallocated after it was used by a pod. That ensures that the next pod isn't affected by previous scheduling decision and that resources are not kept allocated unless really needed. If keeping a claim allocated is desired, use "immediate allocation."
feature.author: pohly
feature.userFacingChange: Dynamic resource allocation: when a claim uses "wait for first consumer" allocation (the default), then it will now get deallocated after it was used by a pod. That ensures that the next pod isn't affected by previous scheduling decision and that resources are not kept allocated unless really needed. If keeping a claim allocated is desired, use "immediate allocation".

issueContext.title: DRA: delayed allocation: deallocate after use
issueContext.body:
When a ResourceClaim:
- uses delayed allocation
- does not get created for a specific pod (i.e. not from a template)

then it currently gets allocated and remains allocated until:
- scheduling of a pod fails because the node originally chosen for the allocation isn't suitable, in which case the scheduler triggers deallocation via `claim.status.deallocationRequested`
- the user deletes the claim

What we want instead is that deallocation gets triggered when the last user of such an allocated claim gets removed from `claim.status.reservedFor`. To avoid races, deallocation must be done through `deallocationRequested`.

This can be implemented either as a controller or directly in the API server.

enrichment.problem: ResourceClaims using the default "wait for first consumer" (delayed) allocation remained allocated after a pod finished using them, causing subsequent pods to be constrained by previous allocations and potentially leading to resource waste or scheduling failures.
enrichment.affected: Workloads that use Dynamic Resource Allocation with the default "wait for first consumer" mode, including pods that create or consume ResourceClaims via CSI drivers.
enrichment.fix: Implemented automatic deallocation of delayed‑allocation ResourceClaims once the last pod that reserved the claim is removed. The claim is now freed via the `deallocationRequested` flag, allowing fresh allocation for the next consumer. Users who need the claim to stay allocated can switch to "immediate allocation".
enrichment.impact: Ensures that resources are not unnecessarily held, improving node resource utilization and reducing scheduling conflicts for workloads that rely on Dynamic Resource Allocation. It also makes behavior more predictable, but clusters using delayed allocation must adopt the new semantics or switch to immediate allocation if they rely on claim persistence.

feature.description: New staging repo has been created for the `EndpointSlice` reconciler.
feature.author: mskrocki
feature.userFacingChange: New staging repo has been created for the EndpointSlice reconciler.

enrichment.problem: The EndpointSlice reconciler was built only in the main repository, making its development, testing, and release processes less isolated and harder to manage.
enrichment.affected: Developers and clusters that use the EndpointSlice controller (part of kube-controller-manager) benefit from more reliable updates and testing.
enrichment.fix: A dedicated staging repository has been created for the EndpointSlice reconciler, separating its code and CI pipeline from the main repo.
enrichment.impact: Allows independent testing and faster iteration of the EndpointSlice controller, improving stability and release velocity for networking features that rely on EndpointSlices.

feature.description:
Hashing of KeyID in Logs

This release adds a feature to hash the `KeyID` values in the logs. The `KeyID` values are sensitive information that should not be exposed in plain text in the logs. By hashing the `KeyID` values, we can protect the confidentiality of the data while still being able to log the necessary information.
feature.author: nilekhc
feature.userFacingChange:
Hashing of KeyID in Logs

This release adds a feature to hash the `KeyID` values in the logs. The `KeyID` values are sensitive information that should not be exposed in plain text in the logs. By hashing the `KeyID` values, we can protect the confidentiality of the data while still being able to log the necessary information.

issueContext.title: [KMSv2] hash the key ID in gRPC interface abstraction

enrichment.problem: KeyID values were logged in plain text, exposing sensitive credential identifiers in log files.
enrichment.affected: Any component that logs KMSv2 KeyID values, primarily the kube-apiserver (API machinery) and related authentication flows.
enrichment.fix: The code now hashes KeyID values before writing them to logs, preserving the ability to reference the identifier via its hash while keeping the raw value confidential.
enrichment.impact: Reduces the risk of secret leakage through log collection, storage, or analysis tools, improving overall cluster security without breaking existing logging or monitoring workflows.

feature.description: kube-proxy service health returns http header `X-Load-Balancing-Endpoint-Weight` with number of local endpoints. The same information is still available in response body JSON `payload.LocalEndpoints`.
feature.author: cezarygerard
feature.userFacingChange: kube-proxy service health returns http header "X-Load-Balancing-Endpoint-Weight" with number of local endpoints. The same information is still available in response body JSON payload.LocalEndpoints.

enrichment.problem: Consumers of the kube-proxy /healthz endpoint could only obtain the number of local endpoints from the JSON response body (payload.LocalEndpoints), requiring parsing of the response payload.
enrichment.affected: Any system that queries the kube-proxy /healthz endpoint for endpoint weight information—e.g., external load balancers, monitoring agents, custom health‑check scripts.
enrichment.fix: The kube-proxy health endpoint now includes an HTTP header `X-Load-Balancing-Endpoint-Weight` that directly reports the number of local endpoints. The same information remains available in the JSON body.
enrichment.impact: Load balancers, service health monitors, and other tooling can retrieve endpoint weight via a simple header, simplifying health‑check logic and enabling faster decision‑making for traffic distribution.

feature.description:
New Metrics Added for Encryption Configuration Controller

This release adds new metrics to the Encryption Configuration Controller to help monitor the automatic reloading of encryption configuration. The new metrics include:

- `apiserver_encryption_config_controller_automatic_reload_failures_total`: Total number of failed automatic reloads of encryption configuration.
- `apiserver_encryption_config_controller_automatic_reload_success_total`: Total number of successful automatic reloads of encryption configuration.
- `apiserver_encryption_config_controller_automatic_reload_last_timestamp_seconds`: Timestamp of the last successful or failed automatic reload of encryption configuration.

These metrics can be used to monitor the health of the Encryption Configuration Controller and to troubleshoot any issues that may arise during automatic reloading of encryption configuration.

feature.description: The apiserver debug endpoint `/debug/api_priority_and_fairness/dump_requests` has been extended to dump executing requests as well as queued ones.  A column for StartTime has been added to the returned table, with the queued requests having a StartTime of "0001-01-01T00:00:00Z".  The executing requests have a RequestIndexInQueue of -1, and the QueueIndex is also -1 for priority levels without queues.
feature.author: MikeSpreitzer

issueContext.title: Debug endpoint to dump currently executing requests
issueContext.body:
### What would you like to be added?

The currently available debug endpoints for APF are for dump_priority_levels, dump_queues, and dump_requests. These commands provide useful information primarily about the state of APF queues, including the the FlowDistinguisher, ArriveTime, UserName, Verb, and APIPath of requests waiting in queues. To help debug APF-related issues, it would be valuable to provide similar information about requests which have been dispatched by APF and are currently occupying 1 or more seats. The existing commands for dump_priority_levels and dump_queues give a count for the number of executing requests per PriorityLevelConfiguration or queue but there is not enough information available to identify which requests those are without also using information available from audit or apiserver logs.

### Why is this needed?

This new debug command, which could be called something like dump_executing_requests, could assist with live-debugging of APF issues. Situations where this would be useful:
1. General APF debugging to see which problematic requests are using a majority of seats per PriorityLevelConfiguration. This would aid in live-debugging in situations where the given request type is not included in the cluster's audit policy or if verbose apiserver logging is not enabled. Situations where a relatively low number of requests use a large number of seats could be debugged quicker (for example if listing 100k+ event objects is taking around 60 seconds).
2. APF issues with stuck requests. For example, this previous issue with broken CRD could've been quickly reproduced if we knew which watch request was stuck executing, https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/109603. A related issue that is still possible is issuing a watch request against a resource with an uninitialized watch-cache and this request will occupy an inflight request until the client drops the request or the watch-cache initializes. The audit event for the watch request wil

enrichment.problem: The existing APF debug endpoint only reported queued requests, providing no visibility into requests that were already executing and holding seats, making it hard to debug performance or fairness issues.
enrichment.affected: Clusters using API Priority and Fairness (APF) for request throttling; administrators needing to debug slow or starved API calls.
enrichment.fix: The /debug/api_priority_and_fairness/dump_requests endpoint now also lists executing requests. It adds a StartTime column (queued requests show a zero timestamp), and marks executing requests with RequestIndexInQueue = -1 and QueueIndex = -1 for priority levels without queues.
enrichment.impact: Admins and developers can now see which in‑flight requests are consuming API server capacity without needing audit logs or increased verbosity, speeding up troubleshooting of APF-related latency or starvation problems.

feature.description: kubelet: plugins for dynamic resource allocation may use the `v1alpha3` API instead of v1alpha2 if they want to do prepare/unprepare operations in batches.
feature.author: pohly

enrichment.problem: Dynamic resource allocation plugins could only use the v1alpha2 API, which did not support batch prepare/unprepare operations, limiting efficiency and increasing overhead.
enrichment.affected: Dynamic resource allocation (device) plugins that interact with the kubelet. Cluster administrators using such plugins are affected.
enrichment.fix: Kubelet now accepts the newer v1alpha3 API for dynamic resource allocation plugins, allowing them to perform prepare and unprepare calls in batches.
enrichment.impact: Enables more efficient resource management for plugins, reduces API call overhead, and improves scalability of workloads that rely on dynamic resources.

feature.description: Faster scheduling when `ResourceClaims` are involved.
feature.author: pohly
feature.userFacingChange: faster scheduling when ResourceClaims are involved

enrichment.problem: Scheduling latency increased when pods used ResourceClaims, causing slower pod placement for workloads that rely on the Generic Resource API.
enrichment.affected: Clusters that use ResourceClaims (e.g., workloads employing the Generic Resource API) experienced slower scheduling; the change benefits any pod that includes a ResourceClaim in its spec.
enrichment.fix: Optimized the scheduler's handling of ResourceClaims, reducing the amount of work and API calls needed during the scheduling cycle, resulting in faster scheduling decisions when ResourceClaims are present.
enrichment.impact: Pods that request ResourceClaims are now scheduled more quickly, improving overall cluster throughput and reducing wait times for workloads that depend on dynamic resource allocation.

issueContext.title: Promoting some flowcontrol metrics to Beta
issueContext.body:
### What would you like to be added?

Some flowcontrol metrics in kube-apiserver have been around for a long time and are very high value signals for how APF is impacting apiserver latency. With APF graduated to Beta in 1.20 and on-going work to get to GA, I wanted to open an issue to discuss graduating some of these metrics to Beta ([or Stable because we skip Beta?](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/blob/master/keps/sig-instrumentation/1209-metrics-stability/kubernetes-control-plane-metrics-stability.md#beta-stability-level)), specifically ones that are high value signals for apiserver latency with many users depending on them already. Here are metrics that I personally think would benefit from graduation to Stable based on their usage at Google:
* request_wait_duration_seconds
* request_concurrency_in_use
* request_concurrency_limit
* rejected_requests_total
* dispatched_requests_total
* current_inqueue_requests
* current_executing_requests 

For other metrics, I propose we leave as alpha for now as they pertain to internals details of APF that most users will likely not care about and mostly catered to maintainers who are looking to optimize implementation details.

### Why is this needed?

Promoting widely adopted metrics to Beta/Stable will provide stronger guarantees on their compatibility going forward.

enrichment.problem: The apiserver flowcontrol metrics were only at Alpha stability, offering no compatibility guarantees, which made it risky for users and monitoring tooling that depended on these high‑value latency signals.
enrichment.affected: Cluster administrators and observability systems that scrape kube‑apiserver metrics to monitor API request latency and flow‑control behavior.
enrichment.fix: Promoted the seven flowcontrol metrics (request wait duration, current executing seats, nominal limit seats, rejected requests total, dispatched requests total, current in‑queue requests, current executing requests) to Beta stability in the kube-apiserver.
enrichment.impact: Provides stronger backward‑compatibility guarantees for these widely‑used metrics, allowing operators, observability platforms, and debugging tools to rely on them for performance monitoring, alerting, and capacity planning without fear of breaking changes.

issueContext.title: Allow for more flexible retry logic with Cloud Controller Manager
issueContext.body:
<!-- Please only use this template for submitting enhancement requests -->

**What would you like to be added**:
Currently, CCM uses exponential backoff when failing to process a service change. It would be great if this behavior—not only the minimum and maximum delay values—could be adjusted if needed.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/8508875e4d400c1454561aa6d879860984bcdf59/pkg/controller/service/controller.go#L54-L58
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/8508875e4d400c1454561aa6d879860984bcdf59/pkg/controller/service/controller.go#L150

**Why is this needed**:
It is possible to change the minimum and maximum delay values but in some cases that's not enough. Changing those values affects all kinds of service changes, and it would be great if it were possible to adjust that behavior in specific circumstances.

Take for example a new Load Balancer being created. We might want to reduce the max retry delay to just a few seconds long so it's ready within the cluster with minimal delay, but for other types of sync failures, keep the max retry delay set to 5 minutes as to not overload the API endpoint that is being polled.

/sig cloud-provider

/cc @timoreimann — Timo, could you please take a look and make sure this is in line with what we discussed?

enrichment.problem: The Cloud Controller Manager used a fixed exponential backoff for load-balancer operations, offering only global min/max delay settings. Users could not lower the retry period for fast‑path LB creation or adjust it per‑scenario, leading to unnecessary delays or API overload.
enrichment.affected: Clusters that use LoadBalancer type Services with a cloud provider managed by the Cloud Controller Manager. Particularly workloads relying on timely LB provisioning or those hitting API rate limits.
enrichment.fix: Introduced a configurable retry period for cloud load‑balancer operations, allowing operators to set custom backoff parameters (e.g., max retry delay) via the CCM configuration/flags. This enables fine‑grained control over how quickly the controller retries LB creation or other LB‑related sync failures.
enrichment.impact: Operators can now reduce the time it takes for new LoadBalancer services to become ready, improving user experience and service availability while also preventing excessive polling of cloud APIs in error scenarios. Overall cluster responsiveness and cloud‑API usage are better managed.

apiChange.description:
`client-go`: Improved memory use of reflector caches when watching large numbers
of objects which do not change frequently.
apiChange.author: sxllwx
apiChange.userFacingChange: client-go: Improved memory use of reflector caches when watching large numbers of objects which do not change frequently

issueContext.title: Reflector retains initial list result for a long time
issueContext.body:
### What happened?

The result of initial list in Reflector is kept in the memory until the last element in the items list hasn't been changed. 

In practice this can be a long time, e.g. there can be some stable pod that are running for days, in configmaps there is a kube-root-ca.crt which stays there forever.

This problem is described here: https://go.dev/blog/slices-intro#a-possible-gotcha

IIUC this affects both:
* clients using informers/Reflectors
* kube-apiserver which is using the same Reflector to initialize watch cache

This means e.g. when all (but 1) elements are frequently updated, the memory usage is 2x the state size (the initial size + current size).

### What did you expect to happen?

When the objects are deleted from the cluster, the memory consumption of the Reflector drops.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

* Create cluster with 1GB state of significant size (e.g. by creating 1000 configmaps of size 1M each)
* Start informer (e.g. I was using https://gist.github.com/mborsz/8964c84b298ee63c7153190d608a7464)
* Observe memory usage (it should be around ~1GB as expected)
  * Sample [pprof](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/2559168/197553760-cfd8a8f0-0996-4ee7-8f8c-5ea72e06bf8d.png)
* Remove 99% of the state
* [issue] Observe memory usage (it stays around ~1GB, despite state taking ~10M)
  * Sample [pprof](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/2559168/197555163-adff7e50-e0db-4c75-8397-929b08dc9c08.png)
* Recreate the state (with the same name)
* [issue] The memory usage grows to ~2G
  * Sample [pprof](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/2559168/197557325-f3aef1f3-c003-4f17-83db-5aac06ab5643.png)


### Anything else we need to know?

This seems to be consequence of the:
* ConfigMapList using []ConfigMap type (not []*ConfigMap)
* Reflector taking pointer to those objects https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/fe9d04763b94366a7a80a1ef3d9f83337eac722e/stag

enrichment.problem: Reflector kept the initial list result in memory until each item changed, causing the cache to retain a copy of the full state. For large, mostly static objects this doubled memory usage, affecting clients using informers and the kube-apiserver watch cache.
enrichment.affected: Any component that uses client-go informers or the kube-apiserver watch cache, such as custom controllers, controller-manager, and the API server itself, especially in clusters with large numbers of static objects.
enrichment.fix: client-go was updated to release the initial list slice earlier / avoid retaining it, improving the memory efficiency of reflector caches when watching large numbers of infrequently changing objects.
enrichment.impact: Reduces memory consumption for informers and the API server watch cache, preventing unnecessary RAM usage and potential OOM situations in clusters with many stable resources (e.g., configmaps, pods).

apiChange.description: NodeVolumeLimits implement the `PreFilter` extension point for skipping the Filter phase if the Pod doesn't use volumes with limits.

issueContext.title: Optimize NodeVolumeLimits plugin
issueContext.body:
### What would you like to be added?

For pods that only use secrets and configmaps, this plugin adds some overhead at scale. @msau42  does this plugin need to run for those types of volumes at all? If not, we can add a PreFilter to evaluate if Filter can exit early.

### Why is this needed?

Improve performance at scale.

/sig scheduling
/sig storage

enrichment.problem: The NodeVolumeLimits scheduler plugin ran its Filter phase for every pod, even those that only used secrets or configmaps and thus never needed volume limit checks, adding unnecessary overhead at scale.
enrichment.affected: Pods that use only secret or configmap volumes; large clusters where the NodeVolumeLimits plugin contributed noticeable scheduling overhead.
enrichment.fix: Implemented the PreFilter extension point in NodeVolumeLimits so that the plugin can skip the Filter phase when a pod does not use any volumes with limits, effectively short‑circuiting the plugin for such pods.
enrichment.impact: Reduces scheduling latency and CPU usage for clusters with many pods that only use secret/configmap volumes, improving overall scheduler performance without affecting pods that require volume limit enforcement.

apiChange.author: yt2985
apiChange.userFacingChange: kube-controller-manager: The `LegacyServiceAccountTokenCleanUp` feature gate is now available as alpha (off by default). When enabled, the `legacy-service-account-token-cleaner` controller loop removes service account token secrets that have not been used in the time specified by `--legacy-service-account-token-clean-up-period` (defaulting to one year), **and are** referenced from the `.secrets` list of a ServiceAccount object, **and are not** referenced from pods.

apiChange.description: Removed `resizeStatus` enum from `pvc.Status` and replaced with `AllocatedResourceStatus`.

apiChange.description: The new feature gate "SidecarContainers" is now available. This feature introduces sidecar containers, a new type of init container that starts before other containers but remains running for the full duration of the pod's lifecycle and will not block pod termination.
apiChange.author: gjkim42

enrichment.problem: Kubernetes had no built‑in way to run a container that starts before the main containers (like an init container) but continues to run for the entire lifetime of the pod and does not block pod termination, forcing users to implement custom work‑arounds.
enrichment.affected: Workloads that require auxiliary containers to run alongside the main application, such as logging, monitoring, or sidecar‑based service meshes, and developers who previously used custom init‑container work‑arounds.
enrichment.fix: Introduces the "SidecarContainers" feature gate. When enabled, a new sidecar container type can be defined in a pod spec; sidecars are started before regular containers, stay alive for the whole pod lifecycle, and are excluded from termination blocking logic.
enrichment.impact: Enables common patterns such as log collection agents, monitoring sidecars, or pre‑flight services without sacrificing pod shutdown speed, simplifying pod design and improving reliability for workloads that need long‑running auxiliary containers.

apiChange.description: Support for proxying a request to a peer kube-apiserver if the local apiserver is not able to serve it due to version skew or in the case the requested api is disabled on the local apiserver
apiChange.author: Richabanker

enrichment.problem: When a kube-apiserver receives a request it cannot serve because of version skew or because the requested API is disabled locally, it would return an error instead of handling the request, causing failures during upgrades or in multi‑apiserver setups.
enrichment.affected: Clusters using multiple kube‑apiserver instances with version skew or selectively disabled APIs; any client making API requests during such conditions.
enrichment.fix: The apiserver now transparently proxies such requests to a peer kube‑apiserver that can satisfy them, enabling cross‑version request handling and fallback when an API is disabled on the local server.
enrichment.impact: Clusters with multiple apiserver instances of different versions (e.g., during upgrades) retain availability for all APIs, reducing upgrade‑related errors and improving overall reliability of the control plane.

apiChange.description: If using cgroups v2, then the cgroup aware OOM killer will be enabled for container cgroups via  `memory.oom.group` .  This causes processes within the cgroup to be treated as a unit and killed simultaneously in the event of an OOM kill on any process in the cgroup.
apiChange.author: tzneal

issueContext.title: [SIG-Node]  Cgroups v2 memory.oom.group support (kill all pids in a pod on oom)
issueContext.body:
### What would you like to be added?

Follow up on meeting of 28-03-2022 [Meeting notes](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1Ne57gvidMEWXR70OxxnRkYquAoMpt56o75oZtg-OeBg/edit#heading=h.2cz4ars29skh) - [Slack thread](https://kubernetes.slack.com/archives/C0BP8PW9G/p1679649131585659)

In the meeting was specified that this most likely won't need a KEP and should be started with a Issue

I see that the kernel in cgroups v2 has an option memory.oom.group which would make all the pids of a given container to get killed on OOM:
```
+  memory.oom.group
+	A read-write single value file which exists on non-root
+	cgroups.  The default value is "0".
+
+	Determines whether the cgroup should be treated as a single
+	unit by the OOM killer. If set, the cgroup and its descendants
+	are killed together or not at all. This can be used to avoid
+	partial kills to guarantee workload integrity.
+
+	Tasks with the OOM protection (oom_score_adj set to -1000)
+	are treated as an exception and are never killed.
+
+	If the OOM killer is invoked in a cgroup, it's not going
+	to kill any tasks outside of this cgroup, regardless
+	memory.oom.group values of ancestor cgroups.
```
@mrunalp  @SergeyKanzhelev 

### Why is this needed?

Some workloads that fork the process in the container, when the OOM kicks in, it kills only one process of the cgroup, causing a lot of noise due to process failures but health checks being successfull. We think that for our scenarios, killing all the pids in the containter would be better.

enrichment.problem: With cgroups v2, the OOM killer only terminates individual processes inside a container. For workloads that fork multiple processes, an OOM event could kill a single process while the rest of the pod continues to run, causing partial failures and noisy health‑check behaviour.
enrichment.affected: Pods/containers that use cgroups v2 on Kubernetes nodes, especially those that spawn multiple processes within a single container.
enrichment.fix: Kubelet now enables the cgroup‑aware OOM killer for container cgroups by setting the `memory.oom.group` file. When any process in the cgroup triggers an OOM, the kernel kills the entire cgroup, i.e., all PIDs of the pod, as a unit.
enrichment.impact: Pods running on nodes with cgroups v2 will have all their processes terminated together on an OOM event, preserving workload integrity and eliminating spurious partial failures. This improves reliability for multi‑process containers and simplifies troubleshooting.

apiChange.description: kube-proxy: added `--logging-format` flag to support structured logging.
apiChange.author: cyclinder
apiChange.userFacingChange: kube-proxy: add '--logging-format' flag to support structured logging

issueContext.title: Introduce JSON logging format for kube-proxy
issueContext.body:
#### What would you like to be added:

Structured logging support in k8s allows specifying logging in JSON. Many k8s components like apiServer, scheduler have support for json. This issue tracks adding JSON logging support for kube-proxy.  

#### Breakdown of the task

To get json logging support, changes have to be made in kube-proxy and Kind e2e script (for Prow/CI runs) which uses KubeProxyConfiguration 

1. Introduce logging-format (--logging-format string  ) option in kube-proxy. Currently there is none. ([link](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/command-line-tools-reference/kube-proxy/))
2. Introduce an option in [KubeProxyConfiguration](https://github.com/kubernetes/kube-proxy/blob/v0.22.1/config/v1alpha1/types.go#L104) so that kubeadm/kind can specify logging-format. Whether this "configuration option" is something generic or specific to logging needs input from a kube-proxy domain expert.
3. Update Kind to make use of the above 2 and specify the logging format similar to how we do for control-plane components. 
4. Prow/test-infra CI runs will have json logging enabled for kube-proxy.

#### Why is this needed:
To get the benefits of structured logging.

/sig network
/cc @serathius 
/cc @BenTheElder

enrichment.problem: kube-proxy only emitted plain‑text logs, making it difficult to integrate with log aggregation and analysis tools that consume structured (JSON) logs. There was no command‑line or config option to select a structured logging format.
enrichment.affected: Clusters running kube-proxy that need structured logging for monitoring, debugging, or compliance. This includes CI environments (e.g., kind) and production clusters that forward logs to JSON‑aware logging back‑ends.
enrichment.fix: Added a `--logging-format` flag to kube-proxy (and the corresponding field in KubeProxyConfiguration) that lets operators choose the log output format, currently supporting JSON for structured logging.
enrichment.impact: Operators can now enable JSON‑formatted logs for kube-proxy, aligning its logging with other control‑plane components. This improves log parsing, correlation, and observability in clusters that rely on centralized logging pipelines.

apiChange.description: Supported `BackoffLimitPerIndex` in Jobs.
apiChange.author: mimowo

enrichment.problem: Indexed Jobs could only specify a single global backoff limit, so a failure on one index could exhaust retries for all indexes, limiting fine‑grained failure handling.
enrichment.affected: Users running indexed Jobs who need per‑index retry limits; also components that process Job objects.
enrichment.fix: Introduced the `BackoffLimitPerIndex` field in the Job spec, allowing a separate backoff limit to be set for each index of an indexed Job.
enrichment.impact: Users can now control retry behavior per index, preventing one failing pod from consuming all retries and improving reliability of large parallel jobs.

apiChange.description: Added fields `reason` and `fieldPath` into CRD validation rules to allow users to specify reason and field path when validation failed.
apiChange.author: cici37

enrichment.problem: When a CustomResourceDefinition (CRD) validation rule fails, users only receive a generic error without details about why it failed or which specific field caused the failure, making debugging difficult.
enrichment.affected: Users who define or consume CRDs with validation expressions, and any tooling that surfaces validation errors (e.g., kubectl, CI pipelines).
enrichment.fix: The CRD validation schema now includes optional `reason` and `fieldPath` fields. Validation rule authors can populate these to convey a human‑readable explanation and the exact JSON field path that triggered the failure.
enrichment.impact: Improves the developer experience by providing clearer, actionable error messages for CRD validation failures, reducing time spent diagnosing configuration issues.

apiChange.description: Exposed `rest.DefaultServerUrlFor` function.
apiChange.author: timofurrer

enrichment.problem: The default server URL helper function in client-go's REST package was unexported, preventing external callers from reusing the logic to construct the default server URL for a given configuration.
enrichment.affected: Developers writing custom Kubernetes clients or extensions that rely on client-go's REST utilities.
enrichment.fix: The function `rest.DefaultServerUrlFor` is now exported, allowing developers to call it directly to obtain the default server URL based on a REST config.
enrichment.impact: Makes it easier for custom clients and tools built on client-go to determine the server endpoint without replicating internal logic, reducing code duplication and potential errors.

apiChange.description: Added new annotation `batch.kubernetes.io/cronjob-scheduled-timestamp` to Job objects scheduled from CronJobs.
apiChange.author: helayoty
apiChange.userFacingChange: Add new annotation `batch.kubernetes.io/cronjob-scheduled-timestamp` to Job objects scheduled from CronJobs.

`name := fmt.Sprintf("%s-%d", cj.Name, getTimeHash(scheduledTime))`

to 

`
func getJobName(cj *batchv1.CronJob, scheduledTime time.Time) string {
	return fmt.Sprintf("%s-%d", cj.Name, getTimeHashInMinutes(scheduledTime))
}
`

### What did you expect to happen?

Expected this to be documented somewhere.

This is a breaking change, affecting a known strategy to obtain the job expected runtime. Eg. https://stackoverflow.com/questions/55694707/access-scheduled-run-time-inside-kubertes-cronjob#comment120366156_55694854
